# TypeSOL: the rules and the reference

## Writing TypeSOL

TypeSOL compiles a subset of TypeScript to a Solana program (native SBF) with an Anchor-compatible IDL. Programs live
in `programs/`, tests in `tests/`; `typesol.json` lists the programs.

- Exported functions are instructions; their parameters are the accounts (`Signer`, `Account<T>`, `Mut<T>`,
  `Init<T>`, token accounts, programs) and then the arguments. Account data types are exported interfaces.
- Integers are bigint: `u8` … `u128`, `i8` … `i128` (write `1n`, never `1`; take `u64`, never `number`).
  Arithmetic is checked: an overflow fails the instruction. There is no floating point.
- Import everything from `"typesol"`: types, and functions such as `require`, `log`, `min`, `max`,
  `fixedArray`, `emit`, `invoke`.
- Fail with `require(condition, MyError.Name)` (an exported string enum of messages) or `require(condition, "message")`.
  There is no `throw`, `try`, `async`, `class`, `console` or `Math`.
- An account the instruction changes is `Mut<T>`; one it creates is `Init<T>` (`acct.create(payer, seeds)`).
- Lists: `FixedArray<T, N>`, `FixedVec<T, N>`, `Vec<T>`; read with `.get(i)` and write with `.set(i, v)`
  (`i` a bigint), not `xs[i]`. `map`, `filter`, `find`, `some`, `reduce` work on them.
- Strings are `FixedString<N>` in account data; `Option<T>` (`T | null`) for optional values.

## Checking your work

- `npx --no-install typesol check` (or `--json`) type-checks every program and lists what TypeSOL refuses, each error with a
  `hint` that says what to write instead. Fix those first; they are faster than a build.
- `npm test` builds the programs and runs `tests/` in LiteSVM (an in-process Solana runtime). `npx --no-install typesol build`
  writes `target/<name>/`: the `.so`, the IDL and a typed client.
- The MCP server (`npx --no-install typesol mcp`, configured in `.mcp.json` and `.cursor/mcp.json`) gives the same check,
  the IDL and the docs as tools.
- The language reference: `node_modules/typesol/docs/language.md` (after `npm install`), or https://typesol.com/llms-full.txt.

## Quick start

No install: try TypeSOL in the browser at [typesol.com/play](https://typesol.com/play/).

You need Node.js 22.12 or later and the Agave CLI with its platform-tools, which hold the clang TypeSOL compiles with.
Rust is not needed. TypeSOL is tested with **Agave 3.1.10 and platform-tools v1.52** (clang 20.1.7); to install exactly
those on macOS or Linux x86_64 (Linux arm64: see
[Requirements](https://github.com/typesol-lang/typesol#requirements)):

```sh
sh -c "$(curl -sSfL https://release.anza.xyz/v3.1.10/install)"
# The installer adds this line to ~/.profile, for new shells; this shell needs it now:
export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/solana/install/active_release/bin:$PATH"
# Downloads the platform-tools (about 0.5 GB, up to 1.6 GB unpacked) and prints nothing for a minute or two:
cargo-build-sbf --install-only --force-tools-install --tools-version v1.52
```

```sh
npx @typesol/cli init my-app --name counter   # typesol.json, programs/counter.ts, tests/counter.test.ts, tsconfig
cd my-app && npm install
npm test                                      # builds the program and runs it in LiteSVM, an in-process Solana runtime
npx --no-install typesol build                # target/counter/{counter.so, counter.json (IDL), counter.client.ts, counter.build.json}
```

`init` also writes rules and an MCP server config for AI coding agents (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, `.cursor/`, `.mcp.json`)
and lists them; `--no-agent-files` leaves them out. `npm install` reports advisories (moderate and high) and packages
with install scripts: they come from `@anchor-lang/core` and the Solana web3.js it depends on, which `typesol/testing`
uses to encode instructions and decode accounts, so the tests need it; none of it is in the program you deploy.

Other versions work, but their binaries are not covered by the project's tests: `typesol build` warns once when the
clang is another one (`--toolchain-strict` or `TYPESOL_TOOLCHAIN=strict` makes that an error), and every build records
its clang, platform-tools and host in `<name>.build.json`.

`npx --no-install typesol doctor` checks all of this (Node.js, platform-tools and whether they are the tested ones, Solana CLI, keypair, RPC) and prints the command
that fixes anything missing. Inside a project, `npx --no-install typesol …` (or `npm run build`, `npm run deploy`) runs the
project's own copy; outside one, use `npx @typesol/cli …`. Plain `npx typesol` is not TypeSOL: `typesol` is not the npm
package's name, so where the project's copy is not installed npx would fetch whatever package has that name. Outside a
project (or before `npm install`), `npx --no-install typesol …` therefore fails with npm's `E404 … typesol - Not
found`, which does not mention `@typesol/cli`: run `npx @typesol/cli …` there, or `npm install` in the project first.

To deploy, on devnet:

```sh
solana-keygen new                             # once, if you have no keypair (~/.config/solana/id.json)
solana airdrop 2 --url devnet                 # test SOL for the rent (rate-limited: https://faucet.solana.com also works)
npx --no-install typesol deploy --url devnet
```

or on a local validator: `solana-test-validator` in another terminal, `solana airdrop 5 --url localhost`, then
`npx --no-install typesol deploy --url localhost`. `deploy` checks the payer's keypair, the RPC and the payer's balance
before sending anything, and stops with the command to run when one is missing.

`--template vault` or `--template escrow` starts from a SOL vault or an SPL token escrow instead of the counter, each
with a passing LiteSVM test.

The npm package is [`@typesol/cli`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@typesol/cli). Projects install it under the name
`typesol`, which is what programs import (`import { … } from "typesol"`); `typesol init` sets that up. To add it to an
existing project: `npm install -D typesol@npm:@typesol/cli`.

Deploying again upgrades the program in place. Keep `target/deploy/<name>-keypair.json`: that keypair is your
program's address.

**Your first change.** Open `programs/counter.ts`, add an instruction (say `decrement`, with
`require(counter.count >= 1n, …)` before `counter.count -= 1n`), call it from `tests/counter.test.ts` and run `npm test`.
If the build refuses something, the error points at the line and, for the usual first mistakes (`1` instead of `1n`,
`console.log`, `Date.now()`, a missing import, `async`), adds a `hint:` with what to write instead; your editor shows
the same.

**Where next**
- The language, every type and built-in: [docs/language.md](docs/language.md).
- Tests with `typesol/testing` (accounts by name, plain values): [docs/test-your-program.md](docs/test-your-program.md).
- Coming from Anchor: [docs/migrate-from-anchor.md](docs/migrate-from-anchor.md) maps every construct, and
  `typesol port` starts from your program's IDL; [docs/case-study-escrow.md](docs/case-study-escrow.md) follows one
  program through the port.
- Real programs checked against their mainnet binaries: [Showcase](https://github.com/typesol-lang/typesol#showcase-ports-checked-against-mainnet), with a
  case study each (Marginfi v2 in full: all 124 instructions, the same on 2,081 transactions; Phoenix v1, a native
  order book, the same on 3,575 transactions down to its event bytes; Raydium AMM v4, a native program, down to its log
  lines).
- To mainnet (wallet, cost, deploy, IDL, verification): [docs/mainnet.md](docs/mainnet.md).
- With an AI coding agent: [docs/ai.md](docs/ai.md) (agent rules, [llms.txt](https://typesol.com/llms.txt), the MCP server).

<!-- docs/language.md -->

# The TypeSOL language

TypeSOL is a subset of TypeScript that compiles to Solana programs. A program is a `.ts` file: its exported functions
are instructions, its exported interfaces are account data, and its parameter types say which accounts are checked and
how. The TypeScript compiler type-checks it against `lib/typesol.d.ts`; TypeSOL then refuses what is outside the
language, lowers the rest to C and builds an SBF program with clang, and writes an Anchor-compatible IDL and a typed
client. Nothing runs on chain but the compiled code.

What differs from TypeScript, in short:

- Integers are bigints of a declared width (`u8` … `u128`, `i8` … `i128`, `1n` literals), and every arithmetic
  operation is checked. There is no `number` and no floating point.
- Everything comes from `"typesol"`: no Node.js, no npm packages, no `console`, no `Math`.
- No `class`, `async`, `throw` or `try`: a failed `require` (or check, or overflow) ends the instruction and fails the
  whole transaction, whose changes the runtime discards.
- Every type's layout is known when the program compiles. Locals and struct fields have a fixed size: strings in
  accounts are `FixedString<N>`, lists are `FixedArray` or `FixedVec`. What varies in length is a `string` or `Vec`
  argument (read in place from the instruction data), a `Vec` field (the account grows) and a string built at run time
  (on the heap). There are no dynamic objects.

For a tour, start with the [README](../README.md); to port an Anchor program, [migrate from
Anchor](migrate-from-anchor.md). New to Solana? [Language basics](language-basics.md#solana-in-a-dozen-lines) starts
with the terms the guide uses.

## The guide

Read in order, or jump to what you need. Every example on these pages is a complete program that compiles, unless it
is marked as a fragment.

| Page | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| [Language basics](language-basics.md) | Solana in a dozen lines, then what a program is: the file, imports, instructions, account data, helpers, constants, multiple files, what the compiler derives, stack and heap, limits and costs (rent, compute, transaction and account sizes) |
| [Types](language-types.md) | integers and checked arithmetic, casts, `u256`, booleans, `Pubkey`, strings, enums, data enums, structs, `Option`, lists, `f64`, heap values, with their bytes and limits |
| [Statements and functions](language-statements.md) | which TypeScript is TypeSOL: declarations, copies and references, control flow, destructuring, helpers, `Inout<T>`, closures, generics, and what is refused |
| [Accounts](language-accounts.md) | account parameters and the checks they emit, creating, closing and resizing accounts, constraints, optional accounts, account groups, remaining accounts, account layouts |
| [PDAs](language-pdas.md) | seeds, bumps, `Seeds<…>`, `requirePda`, deriving addresses, signing as a PDA, PDAs in the IDL |
| [Errors, logs, events and return values](language-errors-events.md) | `require`, error enums and codes, `log`, `emit`, `emitCpi`, return values |
| [Calling other programs](language-cpi.md) | the System, Token, Token-2022, Associated Token, Memo, Metaplex and Stake programs, typed calls from an IDL, `invoke`, `invokeInstruction`, transfer hooks |
| [Sysvars, hashes, signatures and oracles](language-chain.md) | the clock and other sysvars, hashing, signature checks, instruction introspection, Pyth, Switchboard, randomness |
| [Porting a native program](language-native.md) | advanced: the `@fallback` entry, raw account views, Borsh accounts, `BigVec`, the red-black tree, byte builders, Rust's panics and log lines |
| [Built-ins](language-builtins.md) | every name `"typesol"` exports, one line each, generated from `lib/typesol.d.ts` |
| [Glossary](glossary.md) | the Solana and TypeSOL terms the guide uses: account, owner, rent, PDA, CPI, IDL, compute units, … |

Then: [test your program](test-your-program.md) in LiteSVM, call it from [the generated client](client.md),
[deploy it](mainnet.md), and when something fails, [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

The error codes are in [errors.md](errors.md); what a compiled program checks for you and what is left to you, in the
[security model](security-model.md).

## Not supported yet

- A struct holding a FixedVec that is both an argument and account data (its bytes differ there, and the IDL describes
  a type one way): declare one for each.
- Growing an account by more than 10 KiB in one instruction (Solana's limit): realloc again in the next instruction.
- `?.` and `!` on anything but optional accounts, Options and a `find` on struct elements.
- Functions stored in a struct, chosen from a list by index, or returned from an instruction.
- A fused `map` to strings: store it, annotated.
- Floating point (by design).

They are rejected at compile time rather than half-supported.

<!-- docs/language-basics.md -->

# Language basics

This page explains what a TypeSOL program is: the file, its imports, its instructions and account data, and what the
compiler derives from them. It is the first page of the [language guide](language.md). It assumes you know
TypeScript; it does not assume you know [Anchor](glossary.md#anchor) or Rust, and [Solana in a dozen
lines](#solana-in-a-dozen-lines) introduces the chain's terms.

## A program is a TypeScript file

A TypeSOL program is a `.ts` file, the entry file, and the TypeSOL files it imports. The TypeScript compiler
type-checks it against `lib/typesol.d.ts` (the package's declarations), then TypeSOL checks that it stays inside the
language, lowers it to C and builds a Solana SBF program with clang. Nothing runs on chain but the compiled code: there
is no interpreter and no JavaScript runtime.

The file is made of:

| Top-level declaration | What it becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `export function name(…)` | an [instruction](#instructions): an entry point clients call |
| `export interface Name { … }` | a struct: [account data](#account-data), an argument, an event or a field of another struct |
| `export enum Name { … }` | a unit enum, or an error enum when its members are strings ([errors](language-errors-events.md)) |
| `export type Name = { kind: "A"; … } \| { kind: "B"; … }` | a data enum ([types](language-types.md#data-enums)) |
| `function name(…)` (not exported) | a [helper](language-statements.md#helpers), called by instructions and other helpers |
| `const NAME = …` | a compile-time [constant](#constants) |
| `type Name = …` | a [type alias](#type-aliases) |
| `interface Name { … }` (not exported) | a [file-local struct](language-types.md#file-local-structs), left out of the IDL |
| `import { … } from "typesol"` or `"./file"` | the language's built-ins, or another TypeSOL file |

Every other top-level statement is refused: `class`, `namespace`, `let` and `var`, and expressions with effects (see
[what is refused](language-statements.md#what-is-refused)).

## Solana in a dozen lines

What the rest of the guide assumes about the chain. Each term is in the [glossary](glossary.md); Solana's own
documentation is at [solana.com/docs/core](https://solana.com/docs/core).

- An [account](glossary.md#account) holds [lamports](glossary.md#lamports) (1 SOL is 10^9 of them) and bytes of
  data, and has an [owner](glossary.md#owner) program. Only the owner changes the data or takes lamports out; any
  program can add lamports to a writable account.
- A program is an account holding code. It keeps no state of its own: what it remembers is in accounts it owns, and
  the [checks on its parameters](language-accounts.md) make sure an account is one of them.
- Every account holds the [rent](glossary.md#rent)-exempt minimum for its size; closing it returns that
  ([limits and costs](#limits-and-costs)).
- A [transaction](glossary.md#transaction) holds [instructions](glossary.md#instruction). It lists every account they
  use, which are [writable](glossary.md#writable) and which [sign](glossary.md#signer); a program can reach no other
  account. If one instruction fails, the whole transaction fails.
- A [PDA](language-pdas.md) is an address derived from [seeds](glossary.md#seeds) and a program id, with a
  [bump](glossary.md#bump) byte; no key can sign for it but that program's own calls.
- One program calls another with a [CPI](language-cpi.md); the [System Program](glossary.md#system-program) creates
  accounts and moves SOL, and [sysvars](language-chain.md#sysvars) hold the clock and other cluster state.
- Work is metered in [compute units](glossary.md#compute-units), with a budget per transaction.
- A build writes an [IDL](glossary.md#idl), the JSON that clients encode calls from; arguments are
  [Borsh](glossary.md#borsh)-encoded, the program itself is [SBF](glossary.md#sbf) bytecode.

## A first program

A poll: anyone opens one at an address derived from their key and a number, anyone votes, and the creator ends it and
gets the number of votes back as the instruction's result.

```ts
import { type Account, type Init, type Mut, type Pubkey, type Signer, type SystemProgram, type u64, type u8, emit, require } from "typesol";

/** One poll: the votes for and against. */
export interface Poll {
  creator: Pubkey;
  /** Votes for yes. */
  yes: u64;
  no: u64;
  closed: boolean;
  bump: u8;
}

export interface Voted {
  poll: Pubkey;
  yes: boolean;
}

export enum PollError {
  Closed = "The poll is closed",
  NotCreator = "Only the creator can end the poll",
}

const SEED = "poll";

/** Open a poll at the address ["poll", creator, id]. */
export function open(creator: Mut<Signer>, poll: Init<Poll>, systemProgram: SystemProgram, id: u64): void {
  poll.bump = poll.create(creator, [SEED, creator.key, id]);
  poll.creator = creator.key;
}

export function vote(voter: Signer, poll: Mut<Poll>, yes: boolean): void {
  require(!poll.closed, PollError.Closed);
  if (yes) poll.yes += 1n;
  else poll.no += 1n;
  emit<Voted>({ poll: poll.key, yes });
}

export function end(creator: Signer, poll: Mut<Poll>): u64 {
  require(poll.creator === creator.key, PollError.NotCreator);
  poll.closed = true;
  return total(poll);
}

function total(poll: Account<Poll>): u64 {
  return poll.yes + poll.no;
}
```

Line by line:

- **The import.** Everything the program uses comes from `"typesol"`. Types (`u64`, `Mut`, `Signer`) are imported
  with `type`; functions (`require`, `emit`) without it. There is no other module to import from: no Node.js, no npm
  packages, no `console`.
- **`export interface Poll`.** An exported interface is a struct. Used as an account's type (`Init<Poll>`,
  `Mut<Poll>`), it is account data: an 8-byte discriminator, then the fields in order, 8 + 32 + 8 + 8 + 1 + 1 = 58
  bytes.
  The JSDoc comments become `docs` in the IDL.
- **`export interface Voted`.** Another struct; this one is only used by `emit<Voted>(…)`, so the IDL lists it under
  `events`.
- **`export enum PollError`.** An enum whose members are strings is an error enum. `PollError.Closed` is error 6000
  and `PollError.NotCreator` 6001, with these messages in the IDL, as Anchor's `#[error_code]`.
- **`const SEED = "poll"`.** A constant, inlined where it is used. Here it is a seed.
- **`open`.** An exported function is an instruction. Its parameters are the accounts the client passes (`creator`,
  `poll`, `systemProgram`) and the arguments it sends (`id`). Each account type says what is checked before the body
  runs: `Mut<Signer>` must sign and be writable, `Init<Poll>` must be writable and is created by the body,
  `SystemProgram` must be the System Program. `poll.create(creator, [SEED, creator.key, id])` derives the address
  from the seeds, checks that `poll` is that address, creates the account with `creator` paying the rent, writes the
  discriminator and returns the bump. The new account's fields start at zero.
- **`vote`.** `Mut<Poll>` is an existing account of this program holding a `Poll` (owner, discriminator and size
  checked), writable. `require(condition, error)` fails the instruction when the condition is false, and with it
  the whole transaction: nothing it wrote is kept. `poll.yes += 1n` is checked: an overflow fails the instruction
  too. Integer literals are bigints, written `1n`.
- **`end`.** Only the creator may end the poll: `require` compares the stored `creator` with the signer. It sets
  `closed`, so later votes fail with 6000, and returns the total. An instruction may return a value: the client reads
  it as return data, and the IDL lists it under `returns`. (The account stays open; `close(account, destination)`
  would delete it and return its rent: [closing and resizing](language-accounts.md#closing-and-resizing).)
- **`function total`.** A function that is not exported is a helper. It takes the account as `Account<Poll>`
  (read-only) and returns a `u64`. Helpers are not entry points and are not in the IDL.

The IDL the build writes describes all of this: three instructions with their accounts (with `poll`'s seeds under
`pda`, so clients derive its address), arguments and return type, the `Poll` account, the `Voted` event and the two
errors.

## Imports

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64, require, u8 } from "typesol";

export interface Gauge {
  level: u8;
}

export function set(gauge: Mut<Gauge>, value: u64): void {
  require(value <= 100n, "level is 0 to 100");
  gauge.level = u8(value);
}
```

- `"typesol"` is the language's library. Import types with `type`, and functions and constants without it.
- A cast is a function as well as a type: `u8(x)` converts, `x: u8` declares. Import `u8` without `type` when the
  code calls it; one import serves as both.
- `import { … } from "./math"` imports another TypeSOL file of the program ([multiple files](#multiple-files)).
- Nothing else can be imported: `only imports from "typesol" and relative TypeSOL files ("./math") are allowed`.
  Imports must be named imports (`use named imports: import { ... } from "typesol"`), not a default or namespace
  import. Names from `"typesol"` may be renamed (`import { log as say }`); names from TypeSOL files may not.

## Instructions

An exported function is an instruction. The client calls it by name; the program finds it by its discriminator.
`export default function bump(…)` is an instruction too, named `bump` like any other: the program has no default
entry point.

- **Discriminator.** The first 8 bytes of the instruction data: sha256("global:<name>")[..8], where `<name>` is the
  function's name in snake_case (`relayIncrement` is `global:relay_increment`), as Anchor computes it. Two functions
  whose names meet in snake_case are refused. `/** @discriminator … */` replaces it
  ([interfaces](language-cpi.md#implementing-another-programs-interface-transfer-hooks)).
- **Parameters.** Each parameter is an account (its type is an account type: `Signer`, `Account<T>`, `Mut<T>`, …,
  see [accounts](language-accounts.md)) or an argument (an integer, `boolean`, `Pubkey`, `string`, a struct, an enum,
  an `Option`, a list). The client passes the accounts in the order they are declared, and sends the arguments,
  Borsh-encoded, after the discriminator.
- **Body.** Before the first statement the accounts are checked and the arguments decoded: a transaction that fails a
  check never reaches your code ([which error a transaction gets](errors.md#which-error-a-transaction-gets)).
- **Result.** `void`, or one integer, `boolean`, `Pubkey`, `string` (a Borsh String) or fixed-size struct, sent as
  return data (at most 1024 bytes), listed as `returns` in the IDL and decoded by the generated client.
- **Failure.** There are no exceptions. A failed `require`, a failed account check, an overflow or a failed call to
  another program ends the instruction with an error code. The whole transaction fails: the runtime discards every
  change it made, in every one of its instructions.

Unlike TypeScript, an instruction cannot be `async` or a generator, and its parameters cannot be optional (`x?: u64`),
have defaults or be a rest parameter. An argument that may be absent is an `Option<T>` the client passes as `null`.

How a transaction reaches an instruction:

1. Instruction data shorter than 8 bytes fails with 100 (InstructionMissing).
2. The discriminator selects the instruction; an unknown one fails with 101 (InstructionFallbackNotFound), unless the
   program has a [`@fallback`](language-native.md#the-fallback-entry) entry.
3. The accounts are checked in parameter order, then the arguments are decoded (malformed or short data: 102,
   InstructionDidNotDeserialize), then the constraints run ([accounts](language-accounts.md)).
4. The body runs.

## Account data

An exported interface whose fields have a fixed size is a struct. As the type of an account parameter it is that
account's data:

```ts
import { type Mut, type Pubkey, type u64, type FixedArray } from "typesol";

export interface Point {
  x: u64;
  y: u64;
}

export interface Player {
  owner: Pubkey;
  home: Point;
  trail: FixedArray<Point, 4>;
}

export function move(player: Mut<Player>, x: u64, y: u64): void {
  player.home = { x, y };
}
```

- An account of this program starts with an 8-byte discriminator, sha256("account:<Name>")[..8] (Anchor's), then the
  fields in declaration order, back to back with no padding, integers little-endian. `Player` takes 8 + 32 + 16 +
  4 × 16 = 120 bytes.
- Interfaces nest: `home: Point`, `trail: FixedArray<Point, 4>`.
- Every field has a fixed size, except `Vec<T>` fields, which make the account grow
  ([Vec](language-types.md#vec)). Each type's size is in [types](language-types.md).
- Unlike TypeScript, fields cannot be optional (`v?: u64`): `optional fields are not supported; use v: Option<T> (null
  for none)`. Interfaces hold plain fields only; methods and getters are refused.
- What the IDL describes (account data, arguments, results, events, an exported struct's field, a data enum's
  variant) must be exported: a struct used there without `export` is an error saying to export it.

Anchor programs store the same bytes as long as the struct has only fixed-size types. Borsh strings, vectors and options
in account data (Anchor's default) need [`@layout borsh`](language-accounts.md#anchors-account-bytes-layout-borsh).

## Helpers

A function that is not exported is a helper: it can be called from instructions and other helpers, is not an entry
point and is not in the IDL. Every function of an imported file is a helper too. Helpers take values, structs, lists
and accounts the instruction has already checked, and return a value or `void`. They need an explicit return type
and cannot call themselves. See [functions and helpers](language-statements.md#helpers).

## Constants

```ts
import { type Mut, type u16, type u64, log } from "typesol";

const SEED = "vault";
const FEE_BPS: u16 = 30n;
const ROOM = 1280n - 34n;
const ON = true;

export interface Config {
  fee: u16;
  room: u64;
}

export function setup(config: Mut<Config>): void {
  config.fee = FEE_BPS;
  config.room = ROOM;
  if (ON) log(SEED);
}
```

- A top-level `const` is a compile-time constant: a bigint, boolean or string literal, `pubkey("…")` (a base58
  address, checked when the program compiles), or an integer expression over literals and constants declared before
  it, in this file or an imported one (`+ - * / % ** & | ^ << >>`, unary `-` and `~`).
- Constants are inlined where they are used, and may be seeds; when a seed is a constant, the IDL records its value.
- A constant with an integer type is computed in that type, every step checked: `const X: u64 = 1n - 2n + 5n` is an
  error (`1n - 2n is -1, which does not fit in u64`), and `const M: u8 = ~1n` is 254 (`~` within the width).
  Division by zero, a negative exponent or a shift past the width are compile errors.
- An untyped integer constant is inlined as its value and takes the type of the place it is used in, as a literal
  does: `const FEE = 30n` stores into a `u16` field, and `const FEE = 300n` into a `u8` one is `300 does not fit in u8`.
- Top-level `let` and `var` are refused: `top-level variables must be const literals`. A program has no global state
  other than its accounts.
- A few names configure the compiler: `HEAP_SIZE_KIB` ([below](#memory-stack-and-heap)), `MAX_ACCOUNTS`
  ([accounts](language-accounts.md#how-many-accounts)), `NATIVE_ACCOUNT_WRITES`, `PANIC_ON_OVERFLOW`, `PANIC_STYLE`,
  `ERROR_LOG_PREFIX`, `PROGRAM_ERROR_LOG_PREFIX` ([native programs](language-native.md)).

## Type aliases

```ts
import { type FixedVec, type Mut, type Pubkey, type u64, type u8 } from "typesol";

type Price = u64;
type Key = Pubkey;
type Buf = FixedVec<u8, 32>;
type Ask = Price;

export interface Book {
  best: Ask;
  maker: Key;
  memo: Buf;
}

export function quote(book: Mut<Book>, price: Price): void {
  book.best = price;
}
```

A type alias is another name for one type, replaced by it wherever it is used: layouts, arguments and the IDL see the
aliased type. Aliases can be exported or not, imported like any name, and name other aliases (the aliased type keeps
the names of the file declaring it). They cannot be generic (`type aliases cannot be generic`). A union of named
types (`type Event = Fill | Place`) is neither an alias nor a data enum: write the variants as object types
([data enums](language-types.md#data-enums)).

## Multiple files

```ts file=math.ts
import { type u64 } from "typesol";

export const BPS = 10000n;

export function fee(amount: u64, bps: u64): u64 {
  return (amount * bps) / BPS;
}
```

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";
import { fee } from "./math";

export interface Vault {
  fees: u64;
}

export function charge(vault: Mut<Vault>, amount: u64): void {
  vault.fees += fee(amount, 30n);
}
```

- Structs, enums, constants and helpers can live in other files. Only the entry file's exported functions are
  instructions; every function of an imported file is a helper.
- Names are program-wide, so imports from TypeSOL files cannot be renamed (`import { a as b }` is refused).
- Error codes number the imported files' error enums first.

## What the compiler derives

From the source alone, a build writes:

- `<name>.so`: the program.
- `<name>.json`: an Anchor IDL (spec 0.1.0). It lists every instruction (name, discriminator, accounts with their
  `writable` / `signer` flags, `pda` seeds and fixed `address`es, `optional` accounts, `relations`, arguments,
  `returns`), every account struct, type, event and error, and the JSDoc of instructions, `@param` tags, structs,
  fields and data enums as `docs`. Anchor and Codama clients read it unchanged.
- `<name>.client.ts`: a typed client ([client.md](client.md)).
- `<name>.c` and `<name>.build.json`: the generated C and the build's record ([cli.md](cli.md)).

## Memory: stack and heap

A program runs with a 4 KiB stack frame per function and a heap of 32 KiB. Locals live on the stack: a list local
holds at most 2 KiB, and a frame that overflows is a compile error that names its biggest locals. Strings built at run
time and a few other values live on the heap ([heap values](language-types.md#heap-values)), which is never freed
during an instruction.

`const HEAP_SIZE_KIB = 64n` (32 to 256) lets the program use a bigger heap; the client must then add a ComputeBudget
`requestHeapFrame` instruction with that size to the transaction.

## Limits and costs

The cluster sets these; the numbers are those at the time of writing.

- **Rent.** An account holds the rent-exempt minimum for its size, (128 + data bytes) × 6,960 lamports: 1,294,560
  lamports (about 0.0013 SOL) for the 58-byte poll above. `create` takes it from the payer, `rentExempt(space)` computes
  it in the program, and `close(account, destination)` moves every lamport, the rent included, to `destination`.
- **Compute.** A transaction gets 200,000 compute units per instruction by default and at most 1,400,000, which the
  client asks for with a ComputeBudget `SetComputeUnitLimit` instruction; past its budget the transaction fails. To
  see where a program spends them, build with `typesol build --profile` and pass the transaction's logs to `typesol
  profile` ([cli.md](cli.md)), which gives compute units per TypeScript line.
- **Transaction size.** At most 1,232 bytes, everything included: the signatures (64 bytes each), the message
  header, every account's 32-byte address (one byte for an account read from an address lookup table), a recent
  blockhash and each instruction's accounts and data. It bounds how many accounts and how many bytes of arguments one
  transaction can carry.
- **Account size.** At most 10 MiB. `create` allocates at most 10 KiB, and an account grows by at most 10 KiB per
  instruction (3016): grow a larger one over several instructions.

TypeSOL sets one more: at most 32 accounts per instruction (5113), unless the program raises it with
[`MAX_ACCOUNTS`](language-accounts.md#how-many-accounts).

## Next

- [Types](language-types.md): integers, strings, enums, structs, options and lists.
- [Statements and functions](language-statements.md): which TypeScript is TypeSOL.
- [Accounts](language-accounts.md): account parameters and the checks they emit.
- A complete program that moves tokens: [`examples/escrow.ts`](https://github.com/typesol-lang/typesol/blob/main/examples/escrow.ts), which `typesol init my-app
  --template escrow` scaffolds with its tests ([tokens](language-cpi.md#tokens)).

<!-- docs/language-types.md -->

# Types

Every value in a TypeSOL program has a type whose layout is known when the program compiles: a fixed size for most,
a length followed by its elements or bytes for `string` and `Vec` (see the table). This page goes
through them: what each one is, how to write it, its bytes in account data and in instruction arguments, its limits,
and the error code when a limit is hit at run time. Part of the [language guide](language.md).

| Type | In account data | As an argument (Borsh) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `u8` `u16` `u32` `u64` `u128`, `i8` … `i128` | 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 bytes, little-endian | the same |
| `u256` | not allowed | not allowed |
| `boolean` | 1 byte, 0 or 1 | the same, checked (102) |
| `Pubkey`, `Hash` | 32 bytes | the same |
| `string` | not allowed: use `FixedString<N>` | u32 length + UTF-8 bytes |
| `FixedString<N>` | u32 length + N bytes | not a parameter type (take a `string`); in a struct argument, a Borsh String of at most N bytes (102 when longer) |
| unit `enum` | 1 byte, the variant's index | the same, checked (102) |
| data enum | 1 tag byte + the largest variant | a Borsh enum: the tag, then the variant |
| struct (`interface`) | its fields back to back | the same |
| `Option<T>` | 1 byte + size(T), always | 1 byte when empty, else 1 + T |
| `FixedArray<T, N>` | N × size(T) | the same |
| `FixedVec<T, N>` | u32 length + N × size(T), always | a Borsh Vec of at most N elements |
| `Vec<T>` | u32 length + elements, stored after the fixed fields; the account grows | a Borsh Vec, read in place |

## Integers

```ts
import { type Mut, type i64, type u8, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Stats {
  count: u64;
  delta: i64;
  level: u8;
}

export function record(stats: Mut<Stats>, by: u64, change: i64): void {
  stats.count += by;
  stats.delta = stats.delta + change;
  stats.level = 3n;
}
```

- The types are `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `u128` (unsigned) and `i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `i128` (two's
  complement). To TypeScript they are all `bigint`; TypeSOL tracks the declared width.
- **Literals are bigints**: `1n`, `0n`, `-5n`. Unlike JavaScript, there are no `number`s: `1` is refused
  (`Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'bigint'`, with a hint to write `1n`), and so are `number` parameters and
  fields. A literal takes the type of the place it is used in and must fit there (`300 does not fit in u8`). A local
  declared from a bare literal, `const x = 5n`, is a `u64`; an untyped top-level constant takes the type of each place
  it is used in, as a literal does ([constants](language-basics.md#constants)).
- **Both operands have one type.** `a + b` with a `u64` and a `u8` is refused: `operands have different types: u64 and
  u8; convert with u64(...) etc.` Comparisons (`<`, `<=`, `===`, …) need equal types too.
- **Every operation is checked.** `+ - * / % **` and their assignments (`+=` … `**=`) fail the instruction on
  overflow (5100) or division by zero (5101); `**` with a negative exponent fails as well (JavaScript throws there).
  Unlike JavaScript there are no silent wraps and no `Infinity`.
- **Bitwise operators.** `& | ^` work on equal types; `~` flips the bits within the type's width (`~1n` as a `u8` is
  254). Both shifts fail (5100) when the amount is negative or not below the width (`x >> 64n` on a `u64`), and `<<`
  also when bits would be lost; `>>` is arithmetic on signed types. Unlike JavaScript, where a bigint shift never
  fails, `1n << 64n` is not a bigger number and `x >> 200n` is not 0. The shift amount, also in `<<=` and `>>=`, may be
  any integer type up to `u128`.
- `++` and `--` are checked like `+= 1n`. Unary `-` needs a signed type (`unary minus needs a signed integer (i8 …
  i128)`).

`const PANIC_ON_OVERFLOW = true` makes overflow and division by zero panic as Rust's `checked_*().unwrap()` does,
instead of failing with 5100 / 5101 ([native
programs](language-native.md#errors-and-panics-as-the-original-reports-them)).

### Casts

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64, u8, i64 } from "typesol";

export interface Small {
  level: u8;
  delta: i64;
}

export function store(small: Mut<Small>, value: u64): void {
  small.level = u8(value);
  small.delta = i64(value);
}
```

- `u8(x)`, `u16(x)`, … `i128(x)` convert an integer to another width. They fail with 4102 (InvalidNumericConversion)
  when the value does not fit: `u8(300n)` and `u64(-1n)` fail, they never truncate.
- A cast is a value as well as a type: import `u8`, not `type u8`, and the one import serves for both uses (importing
  both is a duplicate identifier).
- `as` does not convert. `x as u64` with `x: u8` is refused: `this is a u8, not a u64: \`as\` does not convert (use
  u64(x) and the like for integers)`. In generic helpers `as T` names a type the value already has.

### Integer helpers

| Function | What it computes |
| --- | --- |
| `mulDiv(a, b, c)` | `a * b / c` rounded down, without overflow in the product: u64 through a 128-bit product, u128 through a 256-bit one, u256 through a 512-bit one. Fails with 5101 when `c` is zero and 5100 when the result does not fit |
| `mulDivCeil(a, b, c)` | the same, rounded up |
| `isqrt(x)` | the integer square root of an unsigned integer (`u8` … `u256`) |
| `min(a, b)`, `max(a, b)` | the smaller or larger of two integers of one type |

`Math` is not available (`Math works on numbers; use min(a, b) and max(a, b) from "typesol", which take bigints`), nor
`BigInt(…)` (`unsupported call: BigInt; use u64(x) or another integer cast`).

### u256

```ts
import { type Mut, u128, u256 } from "typesol";

export interface Pool {
  liquidity: u128;
}

export function scale(pool: Mut<Pool>, a: u128, b: u128): void {
  const product = u256(a) * u256(b);
  pool.liquidity = u128(product >> 64n);
}
```

`u256` is for computation (sqrt-price and liquidity math): locals, helper parameters and results, with the same checked
operators and comparisons, `min` / `max`, `mulDiv`, `isqrt`, `switch`, and as a list index (5104 past u64).

- `u256(x)` converts from any integer (a negative one fails with 4102); `u128(x)` and `u64(x)` convert back (4102
  when it does not fit).
- A shift amount or an exponent is a `u128` or smaller (`a shift amount is a u128 or smaller integer`; `the exponent of
  ** is a u128 or smaller integer`).
- Never in account data, arguments, events, return data or CPI data: the IDL has no 256-bit integer (`A.v: u256 is for
  computation; store a u128 (or two u128s)`).
- `log(x)` prints it only when it fits in 128 bits; a larger value fails with 5100.

## Booleans

`boolean`, with `true` and `false`, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `===` and `!==`. One byte in account data and arguments; an
argument byte other than 0 or 1 fails with 102. Unlike JavaScript there is no truthiness: a condition must be a
`boolean`, so `if (count)` with an integer is refused (`expected boolean, got u64`); write `if (count > 0n)`.

## Pubkey and Hash

```ts
import { type Account, type Pubkey, type Signer, pubkey, require } from "typesol";

const ADMIN = pubkey("4Nd1mBQtrMJVYVfKf2PJy9NZUZdTAsp7D4xWLs4gDB4T");

export interface Config {
  owner: Pubkey;
}

export function check(config: Account<Config>, caller: Signer): void {
  require(config.owner === caller.key || caller.key.equals(ADMIN), "not allowed");
  require(config.owner.compare(ADMIN) !== 0n, "owner is the admin");
}
```

- `Pubkey` is a 32-byte address. Compare with `===`, `!==` or `.equals(other)`; `<` and `>` are refused (`< needs
  integer operands`): `a.compare(b)` orders two keys as Rust orders their bytes (-1, 0 or 1).
- `pubkey("…")` is a constant address, checked as base58 when the program compiles, at the top level or inline.
- `Hash` is 32 bytes too: what `sha256` and `keccak256` return ([hashing](language-chain.md#hashing)), with `===` and
  `.compare`.
- In a template string or `log`, a `Pubkey` or `Hash` prints as base58.

## Strings

```ts
import { type FixedString, type Mut, byteLength, log, require } from "typesol";

export interface Profile {
  name: FixedString<32>;
}

export function rename(profile: Mut<Profile>, name: string): void {
  require(byteLength(name) <= 32n, "name too long");
  profile.name = name;
  if (profile.name === "admin") log("renamed to admin");
  profile.name += "!";
}
```

- **`string`** is an argument or literal: a Borsh String (u32 length, then UTF-8 bytes) in arguments, checked as UTF-8
  on entry (102). It cannot be account data (`A has a variable-length string field and cannot be account data; use
  FixedString<N>`).
- **`FixedString<N>`** is a string field with room for N bytes, N from 1 to 10240: a u32 length then N bytes, always
  4 + N bytes. Assigning a longer string fails with 5105.
- What strings support: `===` and `!==`, `byteLength(s)` (UTF-8 bytes, a `u64`), `log(s)`, `+=` on a `FixedString`
  field, and use as a PDA seed (its bytes). A local bound to account text keeps its own copy.
- Unlike JavaScript, `.length` is refused (it would be a JS number of UTF-16 units: `use byteLength(s) for strings`),
  and so are indexing and string methods (`s.slice`, `s.charAt`, …).

### Strings built at run time

```ts
import { type Pubkey, type u64, type Option, log } from "typesol";

export function report(owner: Pubkey, amount: u64, limit: Option<u64>): void {
  const line = `owner ${owner} paid ${amount}, limit ${limit}`;
  log(line);
  let tag = "id-";
  tag += "7";
  log("tag " + tag);
}
```

`"a" + name`, `` `#${n}` `` and `s += …` build strings on the heap (32 KiB; 5110 when full). In a template, a `Pubkey`
or `Hash` prints as base58 and an `Option` of an integer, boolean, `Pubkey` or `Hash` as its value or `null`, as
JavaScript prints it (after `x !== null`, the value). A template is joined in one allocation; text known when the
program compiles (literals, string and `Pubkey` constants) is folded in; `s += …` grows the newest heap string in
place. Tagged templates (`` String.raw`…` ``) are refused.

## Enums

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";

export enum Status {
  Pending,
  Approved,
  Rejected,
}

export interface Request {
  status: Status;
  amount: u64;
}

export function approve(request: Mut<Request>): void {
  if (request.status === Status.Pending) request.status = Status.Approved;
}
```

- A unit enum's members are numbered 0, 1, 2… in order; initializers are refused (`value enum members are numbered 0,
  1, 2… in order; leave out initializers`). Stored as one byte, the Borsh u8 index; an argument byte past the last
  member fails with 102.
- Compare with `===` / `!==`, or `switch`. An enum is not an integer: `u8(status)` is a type error.
- An enum whose members are strings is an error enum ([errors](language-errors-events.md#error-enums)).

## Data enums

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";

export type Action = { kind: "Deposit"; amount: u64 } | { kind: "Withdraw"; amount: u64 } | { kind: "Pause" };

export interface Vault {
  balance: u64;
  paused: boolean;
  last: Action;
}

export function apply(vault: Mut<Vault>, action: Action): void {
  switch (action.kind) {
    case "Deposit":
      vault.balance += action.amount;
      break;
    case "Withdraw":
      vault.balance -= action.amount;
      break;
    case "Pause":
      vault.paused = true;
  }
  vault.last = action;
}
```

- A data enum is a union of object types, each with a `kind` string literal: Rust's enum with fields, Borsh-encoded as
  Anchor encodes one. `a.kind === "Deposit"` or `switch (a.kind)`, and TypeScript narrowing picks the variant.
- Reading a variant's field is checked again at run time: when the value is not that variant, 5112.
- In account data: 1 tag byte then room for the largest variant. In arguments and events: the tag, then that
  variant's fields.
- A variant may hold a `string` (`{ kind: "Say"; text: string }`): such an enum works in arguments, events and
  locals, but not in account data.
- Write a variant as a literal: `vault.last = { kind: "Pause" }`.
- A union of named types (`type Event = Fill | Place`) is not a data enum: write the variants as object types.

## Structs

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Point {
  x: u64;
  y: u64;
}

export interface Player {
  home: Point;
  score: u64;
}

function moved(p: Point, dx: u64): Point {
  return { x: p.x + dx, y: p.y };
}

export function step(player: Mut<Player>, dx: u64): void {
  const next: Point = moved(player.home, dx);
  next.y += 1n;
  player.home = next;
}
```

- An `interface` with fixed-size fields is a struct; exported ones are in the IDL. Fields are stored in declaration
  order, back to back, with no padding.
- A struct literal names every field (`{ x, y: 2n }`); a missing or unknown field is an error. An object literal needs
  a known struct type: a typed local (`const p: Point = { … }`), a field, a helper parameter, `emit<T>(…)`.
- `a.home = b.home` copies the whole struct, as Rust and Anchor do; how `const` binds one is in
  [copies and references](language-statements.md#copies-and-references).
- A struct cannot contain itself.

### File-local structs

`interface Pair { a: u64; b: u64 }` without `export` is the file's own struct, for its helpers (parameters, results,
`Inout<Pair>`), locals and other such structs; it is left out of the IDL. What the IDL describes (account data,
instruction arguments and results, events, an exported struct's field, a data enum's variant) cannot hold one: each
such use is an error saying to export it.

## Option

```ts
import { type Mut, type Option, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Auction {
  best: Option<u64>;
  floor: u64;
}

export function bid(auction: Mut<Auction>, amount: u64, cap: Option<u64>): void {
  if (auction.best === null || amount > auction.best) auction.best = amount;
  const limit = cap ?? auction.floor;
  if (amount > limit) auction.best = null;
  auction.floor = auction.best!;
}
```

- `Option<T>` (or `T | null`) is a value or `null`. Compare with `=== null` / `!== null`; TypeScript narrows it.
- Using an empty option where a value is needed fails with 5108; `x!` is the value, or 5108.
- `a ?? b` takes `b` only when `a` is empty, and evaluates `b` only then; the result is an Option when `b` can be null.
- `===` between options, or with a value, follows JavaScript: `null === null`, and an empty option never equals a
  value.
- `x.home?.field` on an `Option<struct>` gives an Option (empty when the option is). `?.` on anything else is refused:
  `?. works on optional accounts and Option<struct> values (other values are never null)`.
- **Bytes.** In account data: always 1 + size(T) bytes, `{ is_some, value }`. In arguments and events: Borsh, one
  byte when empty.
- `Option<Point>` in account data: `=== null`, `p.home.x` after narrowing, `p.home = null` or `= { x, y }`. Once
  narrowed, `p.home` (or an `Option<FixedArray>`) passes to a helper that takes the struct (or array).
- `Option<FixedArray<T, N>>` fields (Anchor's `Option<[u16; 3]>`): one tag byte then N elements in fixed layouts,
  Borsh in arguments and events.

## Lists

There are three list types. All of them have `.length` (a `u64`), `get(i)` and `set(i, v)` with bounds checks (5104),
`for … of`, and the [list methods](#list-methods). Unlike JavaScript arrays, indexing with `[ ]` is refused (`indexing
with [ ] is not supported: use .get(i) and .set(i, value), with i a bigint (0n)`), and indexes are bigints.

| | Size | Grows | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `FixedArray<T, N>` | N elements, always | no | account data, arguments, locals |
| `FixedVec<T, N>` | u32 length + room for N | up to N | account data, arguments, locals, events, return data |
| `Vec<T>` | u32 length + its elements | the account is resized | account data, arguments (read-only), events |

Which one to use in account data:

- **`FixedArray<T, N>`** when there are always N elements (a board, a fixed set of slots). The account's rent covers
  all N from creation.
- **`FixedVec<T, N>`** when the count varies up to a known maximum (owners of a multisig, at most N). The account is
  created at its full size, so its creator pays the rent for N elements up front and nothing grows later; a `push`
  past N fails with 5104. It also works in locals, nested structs and return data.
- **`Vec<T>`** when the count has no useful maximum. The account starts small and each `push(v, payer)` resizes it,
  `payer` paying the extra rent, so the instruction needs a `SystemProgram`; it grows at most 10 KiB per instruction
  (3016) and 10 MiB in all. A struct with a `Vec` is account data only, not a local or a nested struct.

### FixedArray

```ts
import { type FixedArray, type Mut, type u64, fixedArray } from "typesol";

export interface Board {
  scores: FixedArray<u64, 8>;
  best: u64;
}

export function submit(board: Mut<Board>, slot: u64, score: u64): void {
  board.scores.set(slot, score);
  for (const s of board.scores) if (s > board.best) board.best = s;
  const recent = fixedArray<u64, 4>(0n);
  recent.set(0n, score);
  board.best += recent.get(0n) - score;
}
```

- `FixedArray<T, N>` has N elements, N a literal from 1 to 1000000; elements can be integers, booleans, Pubkeys,
  enums, `FixedString<N>` or structs of fixed size. In account data it is N × size(T) bytes.
- `fixedArray<T, N>(fill)` makes a local array on the stack, up to 256 elements (`fixedArray<T, N>: N must be a literal
  1..256 (locals live on the 4KB stack)`), filled with `fill`. Elements may be structs (the fill built once and copied
  into each slot) or `FixedString<N>`. It may be a struct literal's field value (`{ prices: fixedArray<u64, 16>(0n),
  … }`), filled in place, and written inline it feeds a chain, a list method or `for … of`
  (`fixedArray<u64, 3>(2n).map((x) => x * 5n).reduce(…)`).

### FixedVec

```ts
import { type FixedVec, type Mut, type Pubkey, fixedVec, require } from "typesol";

export interface Multisig {
  owners: FixedVec<Pubkey, 8>;
}

export function setOwners(ms: Mut<Multisig>, owners: FixedVec<Pubkey, 8>): void {
  ms.owners = owners;
}

export function addOwner(ms: Mut<Multisig>, owner: Pubkey): void {
  require(!ms.owners.includes(owner), "already an owner");
  ms.owners.push(owner);
}

export function reset(ms: Mut<Multisig>, first: Pubkey): void {
  ms.owners = fixedVec([first]);
  const scratch: FixedVec<Pubkey, 8> = fixedVec([]);
  scratch.pushAll(ms.owners);
  scratch.pop();
}
```

These show the list operations only: as written, anyone can replace or add to any multisig's owners. The showcase
multisig ([`showcase/mainnet/multisig/multisig.ts`](https://github.com/typesol-lang/typesol/blob/main/showcase/mainnet/multisig/multisig.ts))
gives its `setOwners` a `multisigSigner: Seeds<Signer, ["@multisig"], "@multisig.nonce">` parameter: the multisig's
own PDA must sign, which only its `executeTransaction` does, for a transaction enough owners approved.

- `FixedVec<T, N>` is a list with room for N elements: a u32 length and the room, always 4 + N × size(T) bytes. Any
  field, any number of them, nested structs too. Elements as for FixedArray.
- `get`, `set`, `push(v)`, `pop()`, `clear()`, `.length`, `for … of`. `push` on a full one fails with 5104.
- `xs.pushAll(items)` appends a whole list of the same elements in one copy: another FixedVec, a FixedArray or Vec, a
  Vec argument, the instruction data or a slice of it. It is a memcpy (about 0.01 CU a byte for 1000 bytes, against 11
  for a `push` loop), and fails with 5104, appending nothing, when it does not fit. (`Vec` declares `pushAll` so a Vec
  passes for a FixedVec, but a Vec grows one `push` at a time.)
- `acct.owners = fixedVec([a, b])` writes a whole one (the unused slots zeroed); `acct.owners = owners` copies a `Vec`
  argument or another list of the same elements into it, as Anchor's `multisig.owners = owners` (more than N: 5104).
- As an argument, `ids: FixedVec<u64, 8>` is a Borsh Vec of at most N elements, read like a `Vec` argument (more fail
  with 102).
- In account data, returned structs and events it has its fixed layout.
- **Local lists.** A FixedVec or FixedArray of integers, booleans, Pubkeys, enums, `FixedString<N>` or fixed-size
  structs can be a local, on the stack: `const metas: FixedVec<Meta, 4> = fixedVec([{ pubkey: k, isSigner: false,
  isWritable: false }])`, `const buf: FixedVec<u8, 600> = fixedVec([])`, `const pair: FixedArray<Meta, 2> =
  fixedArray(meta)`.
  - Given another list (`const y: FixedVec<Pubkey, 4> = xs`) it is a copy, as a struct local is.
  - Setting one up costs about the same at any size: `fixedVec([])` of 1280 bytes is about 10 CU (the free slots are
    zeroed by the memset syscall, the elements written in place, also as a struct literal's field).
- **Size limit.** One list holds at most 2 KiB of elements (the FixedVec's u32 length aside: `FixedVec<u32, 512>`
  fits). The 4 KiB stack frame is shared with the rest of the function, and a frame that overflows is reported with
  its biggest locals; a bigger list is a compile error naming its size. [`@heap`](#heap-values) moves one to the heap.
- A `FixedVec<u8, N>` is also a byte buffer: `pushLE`, `pushKey`, `pushBorsh`, `setLE`, `truncate`
  ([byte builders](language-native.md#byte-strings-built-by-hand)).

### Vec

```ts
import { type Mut, type Pubkey, type Signer, type SystemProgram, type u64, type Vec } from "typesol";

export interface Entry {
  who: Pubkey;
  amount: u64;
}

export interface Book {
  total: u64;
  entries: Vec<Entry>;
}

export function add(payer: Mut<Signer>, book: Mut<Book>, systemProgram: SystemProgram, amount: u64): void {
  book.entries.push({ who: payer.key, amount }, payer);
  book.total += amount;
}

export function sum(book: Mut<Book>, amounts: Vec<u64>): void {
  for (const a of amounts) book.total += a;
}
```

- **In account data**, `entries: Vec<Entry>` holds any number of elements. An account may have any number of Vecs,
  declared anywhere: they are stored after the fixed-size fields, in the order declared, so every other field keeps
  its offset (the IDL lists that order).
- `get`, `set`, `push(v, payer)`, `pop()`, `clear()`, `.length`. `push` resizes the account (realloc) and `payer` tops
  up the rent, so the instruction needs a `SystemProgram` parameter (`instructions that grow a Vec (push) need a
  SystemProgram parameter to top up rent`). An account grows at most 10 KiB per instruction (3016). `pop()` of a Vec
  of structs works as a statement.
- A push, pop or clear moves the Vecs stored after it. A reference into one of those cannot be used across it (a
  compile error), also when the reference was made through another parameter that may be the same account: a
  `Dup<…>` pair, a read-only and a writable account of one type, a struct loaded with `loadAccount` /
  `loadAccountMut`.
- A `Vec` is not a local type (`local type must be an integer, boolean, Pubkey, enum, option or string`): use a
  FixedVec.
- **As an argument**, `amounts: Vec<u64>` is a read-only view of the instruction data (`Vec arguments are read-only`).
  `Vec<string>` arguments (Anchor's `Vec<String>`) are views too, each element checked as UTF-8 on entry (102), and go
  back out as Borsh through `invoke`.
- In a `@layout borsh` struct a Vec is Anchor's: anywhere among the fields, held on the heap while the instruction runs
  ([`@layout borsh`](language-accounts.md#anchors-account-bytes-layout-borsh)).
- A struct with a Vec is account data only, never nested in another struct (`Inner has a growable Vec and can only be
  account data, not nested`); nest a FixedVec.

### List methods

On a `Vec`, `FixedArray`, `FixedVec` or `Vec` argument:

```ts
import { type FixedArray, type FixedVec, type Mut, type u64, type i64 } from "typesol";

export interface Orders {
  qty: FixedArray<u64, 8>;
  total: u64;
  firstBig: i64;
}

export function summarize(o: Mut<Orders>): void {
  o.total = o.qty.filter((q) => q > 0n).map((q) => q * 2n).reduce((s, q) => s + q, 0n);
  o.firstBig = o.qty.findIndex((q) => q > 100n);
  if (o.qty.some((q) => q === 0n)) o.total += 1n;
  const big: FixedVec<u64, 8> = o.qty.filter((q) => q > 10n);
  o.total += big.length;
}
```

- `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `findIndex` (an `i64`, -1 when absent), `reduce(fn, initial)`, `includes(value)`,
  `indexOf(value)` (an `i64`), `map` and `filter`.
- `find` gives an Option of the element, for scalar elements. On struct elements read a field: `xs.find(f)!.qty`
  (5108 when nothing matched) or `xs.find(f)?.qty` (an Option).
- The arrow written at the call is expanded into a loop (elements as `list.get(i)` gives them, structs by reference)
  and may read and write the function's variables.
- A `map` / `filter` chain used right away (`xs.filter(f).map(g).reduce(h, 0n)`, `.length`, `for … of`) is one loop
  that stores nothing; callbacks after a filter get the index among the elements it let through.
- Stored (`const ys = xs.filter(f)`), it is a FixedVec on the stack as big as the list it starts from. From a `Vec`,
  give the size: `const ys: FixedVec<u64, 16> = …` (at most 2 KiB; one element more aborts with 5104).
- `map` gives integers, booleans, Pubkeys or enums. Stored with a `FixedVec<Struct, N>` or `FixedVec<FixedString<N>, M>`
  annotation it gives structs (`(o) => ({ qty: o.qty })`) or text, and inside a chain it gives structs when the
  callback names its struct: `xs.map((o): Scored => ({ … })).filter(…).reduce(…)` (one struct per element, nothing
  stored). A fused `map` to strings is not supported: store it, annotated.

## Struct arguments

Advanced: what an Anchor port meets when its instructions take structs, lists and Options as arguments.

`order: Order`, `ids: FixedArray<u8, 4>`, `orders: Vec<Order>` as instruction arguments are fixed layouts,
Borsh-identical, validated on entry (booleans, enum tags, option tags, string lengths: 102) and read-only.

- A struct holding a `FixedVec` that is only ever an argument is read as Anchor sends it (its FixedVec a Borsh Vec, as
  under [`@layout borsh`](language-accounts.md#anchors-account-bytes-layout-borsh)).
- A struct holding `Option`s (at any depth, as Anchor's `BankConfigOpt`) that is not account data is Borsh on the wire,
  an empty Option one byte. Read its values after narrowing (`if (c.rate !== null && c.rate.zero_util !== null) …`),
  an `Option<FixedArray<T, N>>` too (`.get(i)`, or copied whole into a `FixedArray` field).
- An argument may be an `Option<S>` of such a struct (Anchor's `Option<WrappedI80F48>`): a tag byte, then the struct
  when present; read its fields after `x !== null`. Helpers take the struct, not the Option.
- Likewise `Option<Vec<T>>` (or `Vec<T> | null`, or of a FixedVec; Anchor's `Option<Vec<u8>>`): a tag byte, then the
  Vec. Check `x !== null` before reading it as a list or passing it to a helper that takes the list.
- A `Vec<u8>` is `bytes` in the IDL, as Anchor writes it (clients pass a Buffer).

## f64

Advanced: for ports whose events or accounts carry a float.

`f64` holds a 64-bit float as its IEEE bits (Borsh writes those 8 bytes; the IDL says `f64`). There is no float
arithmetic: `f64FromBits(bits)` makes one from bits the program computed with integers (Marginfi's events report
I80F48 amounts this way), and `f64Bits(x)` reads them back. Float literals (`1.5`) are refused.

Every operator with an `f64` operand is refused, since the integer operator would compute on the bits: arithmetic,
bitwise, shifts, unary `-` and `~`, the ordering comparisons, compound assignments, `++` / `--`, and `min`, `max`,
`isqrt` and `mulDiv` (`+ on an f64 is not supported: an f64 is held as its IEEE 754 bits and there is no float
arithmetic …`). Compute in integers and convert at the end. Equality is refused too (`===`, `!==`, `==`, `!=` and
`switch`): equal bits are not equal numbers, as NaN is not equal to itself and `0` equals `-0`. To compare the bits,
say so: `f64Bits(a) === f64Bits(b)`. Copying an `f64` (to a local, a field, an event) keeps its bits.

## Heap values

Advanced: where memory comes from when the stack is not enough.

Locals live on the stack. These live on the heap (32 KiB by default;
[`HEAP_SIZE_KIB`](language-basics.md#memory-stack-and-heap) raises it), which is never freed during an instruction:

- strings built at run time (5110 when the heap is full);
- a `@layout borsh` struct's `Vec` fields while the instruction runs;
- the CPI scratch lists of a program that declares `MAX_ACCOUNTS`;
- a list or struct local marked `/** @heap */`:

```ts
import { type FixedVec, type u8, fixedVec, log } from "typesol";

export function collect(n: u8): void {
  /** @heap */
  const ids: FixedVec<u8, 3000> = fixedVec([]);
  ids.push(n);
  log(ids.length);
}
```

`/** @heap */` on an instruction's list or struct local keeps it on the heap instead of the stack: one allocation per
declaration, reused when a loop declares it again, up to the heap's size, for about 18 CU. Not in helpers, which may
run many times while the heap is never freed.

**Next:** [Statements and functions](language-statements.md): which TypeScript is TypeSOL.

<!-- docs/language-statements.md -->

# Statements and functions

TypeSOL uses TypeScript's syntax and accepts a subset of its statements and expressions. This page lists exactly which:
declarations, assignment, control flow, functions and closures, and, at the end, [what is refused](#what-is-refused)
with the message each refusal gives. Part of the [language guide](language.md).

In short, a function body may contain:

| Accepted | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `const`, `let` | one name each, with an initializer ([declarations](#declarations)) |
| assignment, `+=` … `>>=`, `++`, `--` | checked arithmetic ([types](language-types.md#integers)) |
| `if` / `else`, `? :`, `&&`, `\|\|`, `!` | conditions are `boolean` |
| `for`, `for … of`, `while`, `do … while`, `break`, `continue` | [loops](#loops) |
| `switch` | on integers, enums and a data enum's `kind` |
| `return` | |
| calls | helpers, closures, built-ins, account methods |
| `const { a, b } = x` | [destructuring](#destructuring), one level |
| arrow functions and `function` expressions | [closures](#arrow-functions-and-closures) |
| template strings, `+` on strings | [strings](language-types.md#strings-built-at-run-time) |
| `??`, `?.`, `x!` | on options and optional accounts |

Everything else is refused at compile time with a message saying what to write instead. Nothing is half-supported.

## Declarations

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64, type u8 } from "typesol";

export interface Counter {
  count: u64;
  step: u8;
}

export function add(counter: Mut<Counter>, times: u64): void {
  const step: u64 = 2n;
  let total = 0n;
  for (let i = 0n; i < times; i++) total += step;
  {
    const total = 1n; // a new name in this block
    counter.step = 1n;
    counter.count += total;
  }
  counter.count += total;
}
```

- `const` and `let` declare one plain name with an initializer. `let x: u64;` without one is refused (`declare one
  plain name with an initializer`), and so is `var` (`use const or let, not var`).
- The type comes from the annotation or the initializer. A local declared from a bare literal (`let total = 0n`) is a
  `u64`; an annotation states the type (`const step: u64 = 2n` above) or picks another width (`const b: u8 = 2n`).
- A local can be an integer, `boolean`, `Pubkey`, `Hash`, enum, `Option`, `string`, a struct or a `FixedArray` /
  `FixedVec`. A `Vec` cannot be a local: use a `FixedVec`.
- Block scoping is JavaScript's: a name declared in a block is gone after it, and may shadow an outer one.
- `const` cannot be reassigned (TypeScript's own error). Unlike JavaScript, parameters cannot be reassigned either
  (`"n" is const or an argument and cannot be reassigned`): copy one into a `let`.
- Struct field names that are C keywords or names the generated C uses (`default`, `signed`, `int`, `char`, `NULL`,
  `SUCCESS`, …), or that start with `_` or contain `__`, are refused (`"default" is reserved in the generated C; pick
  another name`).

## Assignment

You can assign to a local, a field of a writable account (`Mut<T>`), a field of a local struct, a list element through
`.set(i, v)`, and `.lamports` of a writable account. Instruction arguments are read-only (`instruction arguments are
read-only; copy the value into a local first`), and so are helper parameters (see [Inout](#inout-parameters)).

Compound assignments (`+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `**=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`) and `++` / `--` are
checked like the operators they stand for.

### Copies and references

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Point {
  x: u64;
  y: u64;
}

export interface Shape {
  a: Point;
  b: Point;
  sum: u64;
}

export function edit(shape: Mut<Shape>): void {
  shape.b = shape.a; // assignment copies the whole struct
  const copy: Point = shape.a; // an annotated binding is a copy
  copy.x += 1n; // shape.a is unchanged
  const ref = shape.a; // an unannotated const binding is a reference
  ref.y += 1n; // changes shape.a.y
  shape.sum = copy.x + ref.y;
}
```

- **Assignment copies.** `a.home = b.home` and `a.trail.set(0n, a.home)` copy a whole struct or array of the same type,
  as Rust and Anchor do.
- **Binding with `const` references.** `const r = acct.home` names the same storage, like a JavaScript object
  reference: writes through `r` change `acct.home`. Struct references are bound with `const`; `let r = acct.home` is
  refused (`bind struct references with const`).
- **An annotation makes a copy.** `const p: Point = acct.home` (or `= { x, y }`) is a local struct of its own. Lists
  likewise: `const ys: FixedVec<u64, 4> = acct.xs` is a copy.
- **A reference cannot outlive what it names.** Replacing the referenced place (`book.bids.set(i, …)`, `pop()`,
  `clear()`, `acct.p = …`) while the reference is still used afterwards is a compile error, because JavaScript would
  keep the old object: `"q" still refers to a.home; replacing it here would change what "q" reads (in JS it keeps the
  old value). Copy the fields you need into locals first`.
- A ternary can pick a reference: `const o = side === Side.Bid ? book.bids.get(i) : book.asks.get(i)` aliases one of
  them, no copy.
- Scalars (integers, booleans, `Pubkey`) are always copied.

## Expressions

- **Operators**: arithmetic and bitwise operators on integers ([integers](language-types.md#integers)), comparisons,
  `&&`, `||`, `!`, `===`, `!==`, and `? :`. `instanceof`, `in`, `typeof`, `delete`, `void` and the comma operator are
  refused.
- **Evaluation order**: operands and arguments are read left to right, as in JavaScript, even when a later one changes
  account data (`v.length + v.pop()`) or a local (`x + bump()` with a closure `bump` doing `x += 1n`, or a list
  callback writing it).
- **Ternaries** run only the chosen branch: `const fee = vip ? 0n : 30n`. Between accounts too:
  `const source = ephemeral ? rest.get(5n) : reserve` picks a remaining account (`rest.get(i)`, a local or
  `RemainingAccount` helper parameter bound to one) or an `AccountInfo` parameter, and the result goes wherever a
  remaining account does (typed CPIs, `readData`, `loadRaw` / `loadRawMut`, `loadBorsh`, helpers taking a
  `RemainingAccount`).
- **`??`, `?.` and `!`** work on options and optional accounts ([Option](language-types.md#option),
  [optional accounts](language-accounts.md#optional-accounts)). `?.` and `!` on anything else, and a method call
  through `?.`, are refused (a `find` on struct elements excepted: `xs.find(f)!.qty`).
- **Object literals** need a known struct type ([structs](language-types.md#structs)); array literals are only
  written inline, as seeds, CPI account lists, a `fixedVec([…])` or a list of functions in `for … of`.

## Conditions

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Tier {
  level: u64;
}

export function classify(tier: Mut<Tier>, amount: u64, vip: boolean): void {
  if (vip && amount > 0n) tier.level = 3n;
  else if (amount >= 1000n) tier.level = 2n;
  else tier.level = amount < 10n ? 0n : 1n;
}
```

A condition (in `if`, `while`, `for`, `? :`, `&&`, `||`, `!`) must be a `boolean`. Unlike JavaScript, there is no
truthiness: `if (amount)` is refused (`expected boolean, got u64`).

`==` and `!=` compile like `===` and `!==`: both operands have the same type (`operands have different types` otherwise),
so there is no coercion for the loose forms to do.

## Loops

```ts
import { type FixedArray, type Mut, type u64, type Vec } from "typesol";

export interface Book {
  levels: FixedArray<u64, 8>;
  total: u64;
}

export function tally(book: Mut<Book>, extra: Vec<u64>, n: u64): void {
  for (let i = 0n; i < n; i++) book.total += 1n;
  for (let i = 0n, j = n; i < j; i++, j--) book.total += 1n;
  for (const level of book.levels) {
    if (level === 0n) continue;
    book.total += level;
  }
  for (const x of extra) {
    if (x > 100n) break;
    book.total += x;
  }
  let k = 0n;
  while (k < 3n) k++;
  do {
    k--;
  } while (k > 0n);
}
```

- `for (init; condition; update)` with one counter or several (`for (let i = 0n, j = n; i < j; i++, j--)`): several
  declarations, and comma-separated updates run in order after each pass, `continue` included.
- `for (const x of list)` over a `Vec`, `FixedArray`, `FixedVec`, a `Vec` argument, the instruction data, a stored
  `map` / `filter` result or a chain. Each `x` is what `list.get(i)` gives: a value, or a reference into account data
  for structs. The length is read again every step, as in JavaScript.
- `for (const f of [dbl, inc])` runs a list of named functions in turn ([functions](#arrow-functions-and-closures)).
- `while`, `do … while`, `break` and `continue`. Inside a `switch`, `break` leaves the switch and `continue` the
  enclosing loop, as in JavaScript.
- Labels (`outer: for …`) and `for … in` are refused.
- There is no iteration limit: loops are bounded by the transaction's compute budget.
- Remaining accounts are iterated by index: `for (let i = 0n; i < rest.length; i++) rest.get(i)`.

## switch

```ts
import { type Mut, type u128, type u64 } from "typesol";

export enum Side {
  Bid,
  Ask,
}

export interface Book {
  bids: u64;
  asks: u64;
}

const LARGE = 1000n;

export function place(book: Mut<Book>, side: Side, size: u128): void {
  switch (side) {
    case Side.Bid:
      book.bids += 1n;
      break;
    case Side.Ask:
      book.asks += 1n;
  }
  switch (size) {
    case 0n:
    case 1n:
      book.bids += 0n;
      break;
    case LARGE:
      book.asks += 0n;
      break;
    default:
      book.bids += 0n;
  }
}
```

`switch` works on integers (128-bit ones too), enums and a data enum's `.kind`, with JavaScript's `break` and
fallthrough. Case labels are literals, constants or enum members (`case labels must be literals, constants or enum
members`). A `switch` on a string is refused (`switch works on integers and enums`).

## Destructuring

```ts
import { type Account, type Mut, type Pubkey, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Point {
  x: u64;
  y: u64;
}

export interface Player {
  owner: Pubkey;
  pos: Point;
  score: u64;
}

export function read(player: Account<Player>, out: Mut<Player>): void {
  const { owner, pos: p } = player;
  let { score } = player;
  score += p.x;
  out.owner = owner;
  out.score = score;
}
```

`const { owner, pos: p } = acct` (or `let` for scalars you change) from a name or a field path: one declaration per
name, read as `acct.owner` would be. Scalars are copies, nested structs are references. There is no rest
(`...rest is not supported in destructuring`), no defaults, and no nesting (`nested destructuring is not supported;
destructure in two steps`). Array destructuring is only for `const [address, bump] =
findProgramAddressWithBump(seeds, program)` ([PDAs](language-pdas.md#deriving-addresses-in-the-body)).

## Helpers

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Fee {
  numerator: u64;
  denominator: u64;
}

export interface Vault {
  fees: u64;
  rate: Fee;
}

function applyFee(fee: Fee, amount: u64): u64 {
  return (amount * fee.numerator) / fee.denominator;
}

function at(numerator: u64): Fee {
  return { numerator, denominator: 100n };
}

export function charge(vault: Mut<Vault>, amount: u64): void {
  vault.fees += applyFee(vault.rate, amount);
  vault.fees += applyFee({ numerator: 3n, denominator: 100n }, amount);
  vault.rate = at(5n);
  vault.fees += at(1n).numerator;
}
```

A helper is a function that is not exported (and every function of an imported file).

- **Parameters**: values (integers, booleans, `Pubkey`, `Hash`, enums, `Option`, `string`, `u256`), structs, lists
  (below), data enums, `SignerSeeds`, remaining accounts (`RemainingAccount`, or the list: `RemainingAccounts`), the
  instruction data (`InstructionBytes`), functions ([below](#functions-as-arguments)) and accounts the instruction
  already checked (`Signer`, `Account<T>`, `Mut<T>`, `AccountInfo`, token accounts, mints, programs). Helpers cannot
  take `Init<…>` accounts or constraint types (`helpers take accounts that exist`; `constraints belong on instruction
  parameters`), and a read-only account cannot be passed where a helper takes `Mut<T>`.
- **Results**: `void`, a scalar, a `string`, a function, or a fixed-size struct (`function at(numerator: u64): Fee`
  above): the caller gets its own copy, to bind, store with `vault.rate = at(5n)` / `arr.set(i, at(…))` or read as
  `at(1n).numerator`. The return type is required (`helper functions need
  an explicit return type`), and a helper with a result must return on every path (TypeScript checks it; a path that
  still ends without one fails with 5114).
- **Arguments written in place**: a struct, data-enum or `fixedArray<T, N>(fill)` argument may be a literal
  (`applyFee({ numerator: 3n, denominator: 100n }, amount)`, nested literals and a ternary with a literal branch too),
  built in a local of its own as `const fee: Fee = { … }` would be.
- **No recursion**: a helper cannot call itself, directly or through others (`recursion is not supported: a -> b ->
  a`). Nor can a closure.
- Helpers are not `async` or generators, and are declared at the top level: a `function` declaration inside a
  function is refused (declare a `const` arrow there instead).

### How arguments are passed

TypeSOL keeps JavaScript's meaning (a callee cannot change the caller's values unless it is given the place to change)
while passing large values by pointer:

- Struct, list and data-enum parameters are read-only, passed by pointer. Writing to one is refused: `helper parameters
  are read-only: declare p as Inout<T> to change the caller's value in place, or copy it into a local first`.
- When the helper also takes accounts, an argument that is account data (a field of a view or of a loaded account) is
  copied at the call, since the helper's writes could change it. A struct the caller owns (a local, a helper's result,
  an instruction argument, return data, or a struct parameter of a helper that itself takes accounts) is still passed
  in place.
- `Pubkey`, `Option`, `string` and `u256` parameters are passed by pointer too (the SBF target passes a C struct as a
  pointer to the caller's object):
  - a helper that writes nothing reads the caller's value in place;
  - a helper that can write (it takes accounts, remaining accounts or `Inout<T>` places) gets a copy taken at the
    call, and so does text a string argument views in account data or in an `Inout<T>` place;
  - except when the argument is one nothing the helper is given reaches: a local, a temporary, an instruction
    argument, a constant, an account's key, the program id or a parameter of the calling helper, passed in place.
- **List parameters.** A `FixedVec<T, N>` or `Vec<T>` parameter takes a Vec argument, a slice of one, or the caller's
  FixedVec of the same elements (a local, a field of a local struct or of account data) with at most N elements of
  room. It is read-only and passed as a view of its elements, by pointer; a list in account data is copied first when
  the helper also takes accounts, as a struct is.
- A helper that takes a struct account as `Mut<T>` can grow its Vec (`push(value, payer)`: the account's size at
  instruction entry is passed along).

### Inline and @noinline

clang inlines most helpers into their callers, so their locals share the caller's 4 KiB stack frame.
`/** @noinline */` on a helper keeps it a function of its own with its own frame (a few CU per call), for work with
large locals of its own (Phoenix's order ids, built after its event recorder's last CPI):

```ts
import { type Mut, type u64, fixedArray } from "typesol";

export interface Out {
  v: u64;
}

/** @noinline */
function third(seed: u64): u64 {
  const xs = fixedArray<u64, 200>(seed);
  return xs.get(3n);
}

export function run(out: Mut<Out>): void {
  out.v = third(out.v);
}
```

### Inout parameters

```ts
import { type FixedVec, type Inout, type Mut, type u64 } from "typesol";

export interface Recorder {
  count: u64;
  last: u64;
}

export interface Log {
  rec: Recorder;
  ids: FixedVec<u64, 4>;
}

function addEvent(rec: Inout<Recorder>, value: u64): void {
  rec.count += 1n;
  rec.last = value;
}

function remember(ids: Inout<FixedVec<u64, 4>>, id: u64): void {
  if (ids.length === 4n) ids.clear();
  ids.push(id);
}

export function record(log: Mut<Log>, value: u64): void {
  addEvent(log.rec, value);
  remember(log.ids, value);
  const scratch: Recorder = { count: 0n, last: 0n };
  addEvent(scratch, value);
}
```

`rec: Inout<Recorder>` is Rust's `rec: &mut Recorder`: the helper gets the caller's place itself (a pointer, no copy:
about the compute units of the same code written inline) and the caller sees its writes after the call, as JavaScript
shares an object passed to a function.

- `T` is a fixed-size struct, a `FixedArray<T, N>` or a `FixedVec<T, N>` (its `push`, `pop` and `clear` included).
- **The argument is a writable place**: a local struct or list, a `loadBorsh` local, a field path of a local, of a
  `loadRawMut` view or of a `Mut<T>` account, a list element (`book.levels.get(i)`, a narrowed Option's value),
  another `Inout` parameter (passed on), or a literal (a fresh value nobody else sees). A read-only one (a field of an
  `Account<T>`, a `loadRaw` view, an instruction argument, a read-only parameter) is a compile error naming what to
  change (`bump() changes p (Inout): "a" is read-only; declare it Mut<...>`).
- **Nothing else may reach the place during the call.** No other argument may share storage with an Inout one (one
  place inside the other; two elements of one list, whatever their indexes, a BigVec slice's elements included; an
  account and a place inside it; a read-only struct argument inside it: pass a copy). An element of a `Vec` or
