`typesol port` writes the account structs, enums, errors and one function per instruction with its accounts and
arguments, each body failing with `NotPorted` until you write it. It keeps instruction discriminators, account names
and error codes. Its notes (on stderr) list what an existing Anchor client would see differently; see
[Account data](#account-data) below. Then, for each instruction:

1. Give each account its real type: `Account<T>` / `Mut<T>` for your structs, `Init<T>` for one the instruction creates,
   token types for token accounts (the table below).
2. Move the constraints from `#[account(...)]` into the parameter types or the body.
3. Port the body. Integers are `bigint`s with `n` literals, and every `+ - * / %` is checked.
4. Test with `typesol/testing` ([test your program](test-your-program.md)), then compare the IDLs, section by section
   (with `jq`): `diff <(jq -S .instructions ../anchor/target/idl/my_program.json) <(jq -S .instructions
   target/my_program/my_program.json)`, then the same for `.accounts`, `.types`, `.events` and `.errors`.

## Accounts and constraints

| Anchor | TypeSOL |
| --- | --- |
| `#[derive(Accounts)] struct Ctx` + `ctx.accounts.x` | the instruction's parameters, in the same order |
| a composite field, `pub pool: PoolAccounts<'info>` + `ctx.accounts.pool.vault` | an account group: `export interface PoolAccounts { vault: Mut<TokenAccount>; … }`, the parameter `pool: PoolAccounts`, and `pool.vault` |
| `Signer<'info>` / `#[account(mut)] Signer` | `Signer` / `Mut<Signer>` |
| `Account<'info, T>` / `#[account(mut)]` | `Account<T>` / `Mut<T>` |
| `#[account(init, payer = p, space = …, seeds = […], bump)]` | `Init<T>`, then `const bump = acct.create(p, ["seed", other.key])` (space is computed; `acct.create(p, […], 8n + 64n)` keeps an explicit `space`) |
| `#[account(init, payer = p, space = …)]` (a keypair account) | `Init<T>`, then `acct.create(p, null)` (the account signs the transaction, as in Anchor) |
| `init_if_needed` | `InitIfNeeded<T>`, then `const created = acct.createIfNeeded(p, seeds)` |
| `seeds = [b"vault", owner.key().as_ref()], bump = vault.bump` | `Seeds<Mut<Vault>, ["vault", "@owner"], "bump">` |
| `seeds = [b"offer", offer.maker.as_ref(), offer.id.to_le_bytes().as_ref()]` | `Seeds<…, ["offer", "@offer.maker", "@offer.id"], "bump">` |
| `has_one = owner` | `HasOne<Mut<T>, "owner">` |
| `has_one = owner @ ErrorCode::NotOwner` (also `address`, `owner`, `signer`, `mut` with `@ …`) | `HasOne<Mut<T>, "owner", ErrorCode.NotOwner>`; `Address<A, "…", E.X>`, `Owner<A, "…", E.X>`, `Signed<A, E.X>`, `Mut<T, E.X>` |
| `close = destination` | `CloseTo<Mut<T>, "destination">`, or `close(acct, destination)` in the body |
| `address = ADMIN` | `Address<AccountInfo, "Admin1111…">` |
| `owner = program`, `executable` | `Owner<A, "…">`, `Executable<A>` |
| `constraint = expr @ MyError::X` (or without an error: 2003) | `constraint(acct, expr, MyError.X)` (or `constraint(acct, expr)`) at the start of the body: it runs with `acct`'s checks, where Anchor runs it |
| `realloc = n, realloc::payer = p` | `realloc(acct, n, p)` |
| `Option<Account<'info, T>>` | `Account<T> \| null`, or `Mut<T> \| null` with `#[account(mut)]` (the client passes the program id to leave it out) |
| `UncheckedAccount` / `AccountInfo` | `AccountInfo` / `Mut<AccountInfo>`: check what you rely on yourself |
| `SystemAccount<'info>` | `SystemAccount` / `Mut<SystemAccount>` |
| `Migration<'info, From, To>` | `Migrate<From, To>`, then `acct.migrate(payer, value)`; the old struct keeps its on-chain discriminator with `/** @discriminator account:<OldName> */` |
| `#[account(discriminator = …)]` | `/** @discriminator <preimage or 0x8 bytes> */` on the struct |
| `AccountLoader<T>` with `#[account(zero)]` | `Zeroed<T>` (TypeSOL reads every account in place: no copy to avoid) |
| `Account<T>` with `#[account(zero)]` (Borsh) | `Zeroed<T>` of a `/** @layout borsh */` struct |
| `#[account(signer)]` on a non-`Signer` account | `Signed<A>`, e.g. `Signed<Zeroed<Multisig>>` |
| `seeds = [multisig.key().as_ref()], bump = multisig.nonce` | `Seeds<A, ["@multisig"], "@multisig.nonce">` |
| `Program<'info, System>` | `SystemProgram` |
| `Program<'info, Token>` / `Token2022` / `Interface<'info, TokenInterface>` | `TokenProgram` / `Token2022Program` / `TokenInterface` |
| `Account<'info, TokenAccount>` / `Account<'info, Mint>` (`InterfaceAccount`) | `TokenAccount` / `Mint` (`Mut<…>` when written) |
| `token::mint = m, token::authority = a` | `TokenOf<TokenAccount, "m", "a">` (2014 / 2015), or `HasOne<TokenAccount, "mint" \| "owner">` when the parameters have those names; `mint::authority = a, mint::freeze_authority = f` on an existing mint: `MintOf<Mint, "a", "f">` (2016 / 2017) |
| `mint::token_program = tp` / `token::token_program = tp` | `MintOf<Mint, never, never, "tp">` / `TokenOf<TokenAccount, never, never, "tp">` (2022 / 2021) |
| `extensions::metadata_pointer::authority = a, …` (with `mint::…`) | `mint.create(p, …, { metadataPointer: { authority: a.key, metadataAddress: mint.key }, … })`: transferHook, closeAuthority, permanentDelegate, nonTransferable, groupPointer, groupMemberPointer and more |
| `#[account(init, payer = p, seeds = […], bump, mint::decimals = 6, mint::authority = a, mint::freeze_authority = f)]` | `Init<Mint>`, then `const bump = mint.create(p, […], 6n, a.key, f.key)` (`null` seeds: a keypair mint; `InitIfNeeded<Mint>` + `createIfNeeded`) |
| `#[account(init, payer = p, seeds = […], bump, token::mint = m, token::authority = a)]` | `Init<TokenAccount>`, then `vault.create(p, […], m, a.key)` (`InitIfNeeded<TokenAccount>` + `createIfNeeded`) |
| `associated_token::mint = m, associated_token::authority = a` | `Ata<TokenAccount, "a", "m">`; `Ata<Init<TokenAccount>, "a", "m">` creates it |
| `ctx.remaining_accounts` | `remainingAccounts()` |
| `#[account(mut, dup)]` | `Dup<Mut<T>>` (in-place accounts only) |
| `sysvar::instructions` (`load_current_index_checked`, `load_instruction_at_checked`), `get_stack_height()` | `InstructionsSysvar`: `currentIndex()`, `get(i)`, `.length`; `stackHeight()` |
| `ctx.bumps.vault` | the value `create` returns, or `acct.pdaBump` |

## Account data

| Anchor | TypeSOL |
| --- | --- |
| `#[account] pub struct T { … }` | `export interface T { … }` |
| `u8` … `u128`, `i8` … `i128`, `bool`, `Pubkey` | `u8` … `u128`, `i8` … `i128`, `boolean`, `Pubkey` |
| `[T; N]` | `FixedArray<T, N>` |
| `String` with `#[max_len(n)]` | `FixedString<N>`: a u32 length and room for N bytes, always 4 + N bytes long |
| `Vec<T>` with `#[max_len(n)]` | `Vec<T>` (any number, declared anywhere, stored after the fixed-size fields; it grows with `push(v, payer)`), or `FixedVec<T, n>`: a u32 length and room for n, always 4 + n × size bytes; in a `@layout borsh` struct, `Vec<T>` is Anchor's own, bounded only by the account |
| `Option<T>` | `Option<T>`: fixed size (1 + size of T) |
| `#[derive(AnchorSerialize…)] enum` | `export enum` (unit variants) or a data enum `type A = { kind: "X"; … } \| …` |

TypeSOL keeps account data at a fixed layout by default, so three Anchor layouts differ: a Borsh `String` is
variable-length (TypeSOL uses `FixedString<N>`), a Borsh `Option` takes 1 byte when empty (TypeSOL always reserves the
value), and an Anchor `Vec` stays where it is declared (TypeSOL stores growable Vecs after the fixed-size fields; a
`FixedVec<T, N>` keeps its place but always takes its full capacity, where Anchor packs the elements and moves the
fields after them).

To keep an Anchor program's existing accounts, mark the struct `/** @layout borsh */`: it is then stored exactly as
Anchor stores it (`FixedString<N>` / `FixedVec<T, N>` / `Option<T>` become Borsh String / Vec / Option, N being the
`#[max_len]`), its IDL type is Anchor's, and the upgraded program reads and writes the accounts in place. `typesol port`
adds it for you. It costs some compute: the account is unpacked and packed in every instruction that uses it. Without it, accounts that use these types need a migration (or a new program) rather
than an in-place upgrade. Everything else, including instruction arguments (`String`, `Option`, `Vec` are Borsh there),
matches byte for byte. A `@layout borsh` struct passed as a whole argument, returned or emitted is Borsh too, so an
Anchor instruction that takes or returns a struct with `String` / `Vec` / `Option` fields keeps its client bytes.

## Code

| Anchor | TypeSOL |
| --- | --- |
| `pub fn deposit(ctx: Context<Deposit>, amount: u64) -> Result<()>` | `export function deposit(owner: Mut<Signer>, vault: Mut<Vault>, …, amount: u64): void` |
| `-> Result<u64>` / a struct | `: u64` / a struct: sent as return data, listed in the IDL |
| `#[error_code] enum MyError { #[msg("…")] X }` | `export enum MyError { X = "…" }` (codes from 6000, in order; `X = ""` for a variant without `#[msg]`; `/** @code 6200 */` before a member for Anchor's `Y = 200`) |
| `f64` fields (events) | `f64`, made from the bits the program computed (`f64FromBits`) |
| `Option<[T; N]>`, structs of Options inside Options (`BankConfigOpt`) | `Option<FixedArray<T, N>>`; a struct argument holding Options is Borsh as Anchor sends it; an event holding one is `/** @layout borsh */` (`typesol port` writes it so) |
| `#[account(zero_copy)]`, `#[repr(C)]` types with `_pad` fields and `WrappedI80F48` | a fixed-layout struct with `/** @serialization bytemuck */` and `/** @repr c */`, `/** @idlName _pad0 */` on the padding, `/** @bytes */ value: i128` for the wrapped number ([zero-copy types](language-accounts.md#zero-copy-types-as-anchors-idl-describes-them)) |
| `require!(c, MyError::X)`, `err!(MyError::X)` | `require(c, MyError.X)`, `require(false, MyError.X)` |
| `require_keys_eq!(a, b)`, `err!(ErrorCode::AccountDidNotDeserialize)` (Anchor's own codes) | `require(a === b, AnchorError.RequireKeysEqViolated)` (or your own error), `require(false, AnchorError.AccountDidNotDeserialize)` |
| `init_if_needed` + `extensions::…` on a mint | `mint.createIfNeeded(…, { metadataPointer: {…}, … })`: an existing mint is checked as Anchor checks it (2024–2039) |
| `a.checked_add(b).ok_or(…)?` | `a + b` (every operation is checked; overflow aborts with 5100) |
| `emit!(Ev { … })` / `emit_cpi!` | `emit<Ev>({ … })` / `emitCpi<Ev>({ … }, eventAuthority, self)` |
| `msg!("…")` | `log("…")` |
| `Clock::get()?.unix_timestamp`, `.slot` | `now()`, `currentSlot()` |
| `Rent::get()?.minimum_balance(n)` | `rentExempt(n)`, `minimumBalance(acct)` |
| `system_program::transfer(CpiContext::new(…), lamports)` | `systemProgram.transfer(from, to, lamports)` |
| `token::transfer_checked(CpiContext::new_with_signer(…, seeds), amount, decimals)` | `tokenProgram.transferChecked(from, mint, to, authority, amount, ["seed", key, bump])` |
| `token::mint_to_checked` / `burn_checked` / `approve_checked` | `tokenProgram.mintToChecked(mint, to, authority, amount)` / `burnChecked(from, mint, authority, amount)` / `approveChecked(source, mint, delegate, owner, amount)` |
| `system_program::transfer(CpiContext::new_with_signer(…, &[vault_seeds]), lamports)` | `systemProgram.transfer(vault, to, lamports, ["vault", owner.key, bump])` |
| `invoke_signed(&ix, infos, &[seeds_a, seeds_b])` | `invoke(program, accounts, data, [seedsA, seedsB])` |
| `let (_, data) = get_return_data().unwrap(); Quote::try_from_slice(&data)?` | `const quote = returnData<Quote>(program)` (a `@layout borsh` struct when it holds Options, strings or Vecs) |
| `[test.validator.clone]` in Anchor.toml | `"clone": [...]` in typesol.json and `typesol clone` (loaded by `testProgram`) |
| `anchor_spl::metadata::update_metadata_accounts_v2` | `metadataProgram.updateMetadataAccountsV2(…)` |
| `anchor_spl::metadata::burn_nft` / mpl `BurnV1` | `metadataProgram.burnV1(…)` |
| `Sysvar<StakeHistory>` / `StakeHistory::get(epoch)` | `StakeHistorySysvar`: `effective(epoch)`, `activating(epoch)`, `deactivating(epoch)`, `has(epoch)` |
| `EpochSchedule::get()?`, `LastRestartSlot::get()?` | `slotsPerEpoch()`, `epochWarmup()`, `firstNormalEpoch()`, `firstNormalSlot()`; `lastRestartSlot()` |
| `anchor_spl::stake::{authorize, deactivate_stake, withdraw}`, `delegate_stake` | `stakeProgram.authorize / deactivate / withdraw / delegate(…)` |
| `RandomnessAccountData::parse(…)?.get_value(&clock)?` (switchboard-on-demand) | `randomness: SwitchboardRandomness`, `randomness.value()` / `valueU64()`, `randomness.seedSlot` |
| `pub fn fallback(program_id, accounts, data)` | `/** @fallback */ export function fallback(): void` with `instructionData()` and `remainingAccounts()` |
| `#[access_control(check(&ctx))]` | call the check first in the body (`check(vault, owner)`), or `constraint(acct, …)` for one that belongs with an account's checks |
| `spl_memo::build_memo` + `invoke` | `memoProgram.memo(text, [signers])` |
| `UncheckedAccount` at the SlotHashes address | `SlotHashesSysvar`: `latestSlot`, `latestHash` |
| `spl_token_group_interface` CPIs (`initialize_group`, `initialize_member`, …) | `token.initializeTokenGroup(…)`, `initializeGroupMember(…)`, `updateGroupMaxSize(…)`, `updateGroupAuthority(…)` |
| `invoke_signed(&ix, &accounts, &[seeds])` | `invoke(program, [writable(a), readonly(b)], [data…], seeds)` |
| `invoke_signed(&Instruction { program_id, accounts, data }, ctx.remaining_accounts, …)` built at run time | `invokeInstruction(programId, metas, data, remainingAccounts(), seeds)` |
| `multisig.owners = owners` (a `Vec` argument into account data) | the same |
| `declare_program!(other)` / CPI to another Anchor program | `typesol cpi other.json` generates typed helpers |
| `for x in v.iter()` | `for (const x of v)` |
| `v.iter().any(\|x\| …)`, `.all`, `.position`, `.find`, `.fold(init, …)`, `.contains(&x)` | `v.some((x) => …)`, `every`, `findIndex`, `find`, `reduce((acc, x) => …, init)`, `includes(x)` |
| a closure `\|x\| x + offset`, `let fee = \|x: u64\| x / 100;` | `const f = (x: u64): u64 => x + offset` (it may read and write the function's variables), `const fee = (x: u64): u64 => x / 100n;` |
| `x.unwrap_or(d)` | `x ?? d` |
| `fn max<T: PartialOrd>(a: T, b: T) -> T` | `function max<T extends bigint>(a: T, b: T): T` (one copy per type used) |
| `fn add_event(rec: &mut EventRecorder, e: &Event)` | `function addEvent(rec: Inout<EventRecorder>, e: Event): void` (structs, FixedArray and FixedVec; a `&mut u64` becomes a returned value or a struct field) |

## Tooling

| Anchor | TypeSOL |
| --- | --- |
| `anchor init` | `typesol init` (`--template vault` / `escrow`) |
| `anchor build` | `typesol build` (writes the IDL and a TypeScript client next to the binary) |
| `anchor test` (mocha, bankrun) | `npm test` with `typesol/testing` in LiteSVM |
| `anchor deploy` | `typesol deploy` ([deploy to mainnet](mainnet.md)) |
| `anchor idl init` / `upgrade` | `typesol idl publish` |
| `anchor verify` | `typesol verify` (reads the deployed program and IDL from the cluster) |
| `@coral-xyz/anchor` `Program` client | the generated `<name>.client.ts` on `@solana/kit`, or Anchor's client with the IDL |

<!-- docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

Grouped by when they happen; within each group, the problems a first run meets come first.

## Install

### `TypeSOL needs Node.js 22.12 or later`

The CLI checks the Node.js version before anything else. On an older one, `npm install` can fail inside npm and the
tests with `Map.groupBy is not a function`; install a current Node.js (https://nodejs.org, or `nvm install 22`).

### `npm error 404 … typesol - Not found`

`npx --no-install typesol` ran outside a project, or before `npm install` in it: `typesol` is the name projects install
the package under, not a package on npm. Run `npx @typesol/cli …` there, or `npm install` in the project first.

### "the Agave CLI is not installed" (formerly "Solana SBF SDK not found")

Install it and its platform-tools as in the README's [Quick start](../README.md#quick-start):

```sh
sh -c "$(curl -sSfL https://release.anza.xyz/v3.1.10/install)"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/solana/install/active_release/bin:$PATH"   # the installer edits ~/.profile only
cargo-build-sbf --install-only --force-tools-install --tools-version v1.52   # about 0.5 GB, quiet for a minute or two
```

TypeSOL looks in `~/.local/share/solana/install/active_release/bin/platform-tools-sdk/sbf` and next to
`cargo-build-sbf` on PATH; set `TYPESOL_SBF_SDK` to a `platform-tools-sdk/sbf` directory otherwise. On Linux arm64 see
[Linux arm64: the Agave installer fails with a 404](#linux-arm64-the-agave-installer-fails-with-a-404).

### `cargo-build-sbf: command not found` right after installing

The Agave installer adds its `bin` directory to `PATH` in `~/.profile`, which only new login shells read. In the same
shell, run `export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/solana/install/active_release/bin:$PATH"`.

### "the Agave CLI is installed, but not its platform-tools" (formerly "platform-tools missing") / "no SBPF v2 libraries"

`cargo-build-sbf --install-only --force-tools-install --tools-version v1.52`. Neither `cargo-build-sbf --version` (it
downloads nothing) nor `cargo-build-sbf --force-tools-install` alone (it needs Cargo and a Cargo project) installs them.

### Linux arm64: the Agave installer fails with a 404

Anza publishes no Agave CLI for Linux arm64 (`agave-install-init-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` is not there), but
platform-tools has a `linux-aarch64` package. With it and the SDK's C files from the x86_64 release (headers and
linker script, as the `--docker` image takes them), `typesol build` and LiteSVM tests work; `typesol doctor` prints
these commands there (they need `curl` and `bzip2`):

```sh
mkdir -p $HOME/.local/share/typesol-sdk/sbf/dependencies/platform-tools
curl -sSfL https://github.com/anza-xyz/agave/releases/download/v3.1.10/solana-release-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.bz2 | tar -xj -C $HOME/.local/share/typesol-sdk --strip-components=3 solana-release/bin/platform-tools-sdk/sbf/c
curl -sSfL https://github.com/anza-xyz/platform-tools/releases/download/v1.52/platform-tools-linux-aarch64.tar.bz2 | tar -xj -C $HOME/.local/share/typesol-sdk/sbf/dependencies/platform-tools
touch $HOME/.local/share/typesol-sdk/sbf/dependencies/platform-tools-v1.52.md
export TYPESOL_SBF_SDK=$HOME/.local/share/typesol-sdk/sbf   # add this line to ~/.profile too
```

Deploying needs the Solana CLI: deploy from macOS or Linux x86_64, or build the Agave CLI from source
(https://docs.anza.xyz/cli/install). `build --docker` (linux/amd64, emulated) works on any host with Docker.

### Windows

Not tested; use WSL2 with the Linux Agave CLI.

### Node errors such as `ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION` or `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`

Use Node.js 22.12 or newer.

### "warning: this build uses clang … TypeSOL is tested with clang 20.1.7-rust-dev …"

The active platform-tools are not the ones the release is tested with (platform-tools v1.52, from Agave 3.1.10). The
build goes on, but the C TypeSOL generates is only checked against that clang: another one can compile it to other
bytes, and what the C relies on includes backend details (how the SBF backend passes struct arguments was behind a
defect fixed after 0.43.0). Install the tested ones with `cargo-build-sbf --install-only --force-tools-install
--tools-version v1.52`; `typesol doctor` shows which are active. In CI, `--toolchain-strict` (or
`TYPESOL_TOOLCHAIN=strict`) turns the warning into an error.

## Writing and running a program

### A build error you don't recognize

The compiler adds a `hint:` line under TypeScript's message where TypeScript's own advice points the wrong way for a
program (and for a global a program does not have, such as `console` or `process`, says so in place of TypeScript's
advice to add a library). The usual ones: integers are `bigint` (`1n`, `u64` parameters, not `number`); `require`,
`log`, `min`, `max`, `fixedArray`, the types (`Signer`, `Mut`, …) and the integer casts are imported from `"typesol"` (a
cast such as `u64(x)` without `type`: `import { u64 }`); arrays are read with `.get(i)` and written with `.set(i, v)`;
an account you change is a `Mut<T>` parameter; the time is `now()`, not `Date.now()`; there is no `async`, `try`,
`throw` or `class`. The full list of what the subset covers is in [language.md](language.md).

### A transaction fails with a custom error

See [errors.md](errors.md). Failures raised by the compiler's checks log their TypeScript location, e.g. `TypeSOL:
arithmetic overflow (vault.ts:42)`.

### "exceeded CUs meter" / "Computational budget exceeded"

The transaction ran out of compute units: by default each instruction gets 200,000, and the logs end with `Program
<id> consumed 200000 of 200000 compute units` and `… failed: exceeded CUs meter at BPF instruction …`. Ask for more,
up to 1,400,000 per transaction, with a ComputeBudget `SetComputeUnitLimit` instruction placed before the others
(`getSetComputeUnitLimitInstruction({ units })` from `@solana-program/compute-budget`, or the bytes `[2, units as a
u32 little-endian]` to `ComputeBudget111111111111111111111111111111`). The generated client's `sendInstructions` and
the testing library's `t.send(payer, ...ixs)` send the instructions they are given, so pass it first:
`t.send(alice, setLimit, t.ix(…))`. To spend less, find the costly lines with `typesol build --profile` and `typesol
profile` ([limits and costs](language-basics.md#limits-and-costs)).

### `Transaction size … exceeds limit of 1232 bytes` / "transaction too large"

A transaction is at most 1,232 bytes, signatures, account addresses and instruction data included. Kit refuses to send
a larger one (the first message), and an RPC node refuses it too. Split the work into several transactions, pass
fewer accounts, or send large data in chunks into an account the program reads; with many accounts, a version 0
transaction with an address lookup table costs one byte per account instead of 32 (kit's
`compressTransactionMessageUsingAddressLookupTables`) ([limits and costs](language-basics.md#limits-and-costs)).

### Heap errors (5110) building strings

Strings are allocated on a 32 KiB heap and never freed. Build less text, or declare `const HEAP_SIZE_KIB = 64n` and add
a ComputeBudget `requestHeapFrame` instruction to the transaction.

### "instruction X (with the helpers inlined into it) needs N bytes of stack; SBPF v0 gives each function 4096"

Under SBPF v0 (the default) every function gets a fixed 4 KiB stack frame, and going past it corrupts memory, so the
build refuses it. SBPF v1 and v2 (`--sbpf v1` / `v2`) grow frames dynamically, so this limit does not apply there. Large
structs and arrays copied into typed locals (`const q: Big = acct.big`) are the usual cause: bind them without a type
(`const q = acct.big`, a reference into the account data). The message lists the biggest locals (clang's frame layout: a
local's name and the source line near it; the locals of an inlined helper show as unnamed, with the helpers' locals that
may be them). Helpers are often inlined into their instruction, so their locals count toward its frame: mark one `/**
@noinline */` to give it a 4 KiB frame of its own (a few compute units per call), or declare a large local list or
struct of an instruction `/** @heap */` to keep it on the heap (about 18 CU for the allocation).

### "… is missing, but typesol.json records …"

The program keypair under `target/deploy/` was deleted or replaced. Restore it from your backup. Without it you cannot
upgrade the deployed program; removing `"address"` from `typesol.json` gives the program a new address.

## Deploy

### `no payer keypair at ~/.config/solana/id.json` (deploy)

`solana-keygen new` creates it (or pass `--keypair <file>`); fund it on devnet with `solana airdrop 2 --url devnet`.
Nothing is sent before it exists.

### "`solana` was not found on PATH" (deploy)

Install the Agave CLI, or use `typesol deploy --dry-run` and run the printed commands yourself.

### `typesol idl publish` fails on a local validator with "invalid instruction data"

The System Program of `solana-test-validator` (Agave 3.1 included) rejects a System instruction that the current Program
Metadata program uses. The error shows the failing transaction's last log lines. No option fixes it locally: the System
Program is part of the validator. Publish where the Program Metadata program is deployed, mainnet-beta or devnet
(`npx --no-install typesol idl publish --url devnet`; [publish the IDL](mainnet.md#5-publish-the-idl)); against a local
validator, clients read the IDL file the build writes (`target/<name>/<name>.json`, [client.md](client.md)).

## Verify and `--docker`

### `typesol verify` says MISMATCH

First make sure the same sources (imports included), TypeSOL version and SBPF version are used. Then the toolchain:
verify prints the rebuild's clang and platform-tools, and the deployed build's when a `<name>.build.json` describes the
deployed bytes (`--manifest <file>`, one next to a given `.so`, or the local build's). A program on chain carries no
such record, so keep the build manifest of every deployment.

### `--docker needs Docker: docker is not installed` / `the Docker daemon is not running`

`build --docker` and `verify --docker` run in a container: install Docker, or start Docker Desktop (or `sudo systemctl
start docker`). `typesol doctor` has a `docker` row. Nothing is built without it; drop `--docker` to build with your own
platform-tools.

### `docker build of typesol-build:… failed`

The first `--docker` build makes the image, which needs the network: the base images from Docker Hub, the Agave and
platform-tools release files from GitHub, the TypeSOL tarball from npm. A `checksum` error means a downloaded file is
not the one the Dockerfile pins (retry; if it persists, report it). `typesol tarball check: integrity …` means the
tarball npm served is not the one `releases/<version>.json` records: do not use that version until it is explained.
`typesol dependency lock: …` means the lock does not describe the package's dependencies or names a package without a
registry integrity; an `EINTEGRITY` error from `npm ci` means a downloaded dependency is not the one the lock records:
the same.

### `the local image typesol-build:… was not built from this release record and dependency lock`

An image of that tag exists, made from a record or lock with other values (it names them). Two records of one version
disagree, so find out which is right before going on; to build from the one given now, `docker image rm` the tag and run
again.

### `no dependency lock for TypeSOL <version>`

Neither this package nor that version's tarball has `docker/deps/<version>.lock.json`: use a later `@typesol/cli`, which
ships the locks of the versions before it. On arm64 machines the image is linux/amd64 and runs emulated: Docker Desktop
provides the x86_64 emulation (QEMU or Rosetta); other Docker installs may need `binfmt` for amd64.

### `no release record for TypeSOL <version>` / `could not fetch the release record`

The container installs only versions whose tarball has a record: the package's own, or `releases/<version>.json` on the
repository's main branch, which `--docker` fetches for a release newer than the package. Offline (or behind a proxy that
blocks raw.githubusercontent.com), pass the record yourself with `--release-record releases/<version>.json` from a
checkout, or choose a version the package records with `--typesol-version`. HTTP 404 means the repository has no record
for that version: check that it is a released version. 0.42.0 and earlier have no record.

### `this project installs typesol X …, but this is typesol Y`

A `typesol` other than the project's ran `--docker`. Run the project's own (`npx --no-install typesol …`), or say which
version to use with `--typesol-version`.

### `the container build failed … the container sees only <dir>`

The compiler's error is printed above it. The container mounts only the project root (or a single file's directory): an
import from outside it is missing there.

### `verify` says `differs   host`

The same TypeSOL (0.44.1 or earlier) and toolchain built the two sides on different hosts. That may be the cause if the
program has 128-bit or signed division: those versions linked platform-tools' compiler-builtins, which each host package
lays out differently. Rebuild on the deployed side's kind of host (or with `--docker`, if the deployed build was one).
From 0.45.0 on the host is not a difference between macOS arm64, Linux arm64 and Linux x86_64 (the hosts measured);
`differs   host (not measured)` means one side was built on another host.

### A 0.44.x program with division, deployed from macOS or Linux arm64, does not match `verify --docker`

0.44.0 and 0.44.1 linked platform-tools' compiler-builtins, so a program that calls 128-bit or signed division built to
other bytes on each host package; the container is linux/amd64 and gives the Linux x86_64 bytes. What verifies it is a
0.44.x install (the version in its `.build.json`) on the same kind of host as the one that built it, without `--docker`:
`npx @typesol/cli@0.44.1 verify …` on macOS arm64 for a build made there.

<!-- docs/mainnet.md -->

# Deploy to mainnet

From an empty directory to a program on Solana mainnet-beta: create, test, deploy, publish the IDL, then check that
the deployed binary is the one your source builds. The program here is the counter that `typesol init` creates
(11,400 bytes, 11.1 KiB, built with TypeSOL 0.45.0 and platform-tools clang 20.1.7 for SBPF v0; other versions differ
slightly); any TypeSOL project works the same way.

**Before you deploy anything that holds value.** TypeSOL has had internal security reviews by its maintainers, not an
independent audit ([status](security-model.md#status)). Do not put significant value behind a program built with it
until an external audit of the compiler and runtime is published, and audit your own program as you would any Solana
program.

You need Node.js 22.12 or later and the Agave CLI with platform-tools (see the README's [Quick start](../README.md#quick-start)).

**The toolchain you deploy with.** The binary is what the platform-tools' clang makes of the generated C, so the
toolchain is part of what you trust. Deploy with the one TypeSOL is tested with (Agave 3.1.10, platform-tools v1.52;
`typesol doctor` says whether yours is, and `typesol deploy --toolchain-strict` refuses another). The host does not
matter from 0.45.0 on: with the same TypeSOL and toolchain a program builds to the same bytes on macOS arm64, Linux
arm64 and Linux x86_64 (measured over 76 programs for SBPF v0 and 14 for v1 and v2; up to 0.44.1 a program with
128-bit or signed division did not, [stability.md](stability.md#what-builds-the-same-bytes-where)). For a program others should be able to verify, build
it with `--docker` (step 2) all the same: a pinned linux/amd64 container that anyone can rebuild, so the whole
environment is one recipe. Keep
`target/my_app/my_app.build.json` with each deployment, next to the commit you deployed: it records the TypeSOL,
TypeScript, clang and platform-tools versions, the host, the container when there was one, and the deployed bytes'
sha256. Step 6's `verify` matches only when it rebuilds with the same TypeSOL version and toolchain (and, for a program
with 128-bit or signed division built with 0.44.1 or earlier, the same kind of host), and on a mismatch `--manifest`
with that file shows what differs.

## 1. Create and test

```sh
npx @typesol/cli init my-app
cd my-app
npm install
npm test
```

`npm test` runs `tests/my_app.test.ts` in LiteSVM: it compiles the program and calls it, with no validator or SOL.
Write your program in `programs/my_app.ts` and keep the tests passing before you spend anything.

## 2. Build

```sh
npx --no-install typesol build
```

This writes `target/my_app/`: the program (`my_app.so`), its Anchor IDL (`my_app.json`), a TypeScript client
(`my_app.client.ts`) and the generated C. The first build also creates `target/deploy/my_app-keypair.json`, the
program's address, and records the address in `typesol.json`.

**Back up `target/deploy/my_app-keypair.json` now.** It is not committed (`.gitignore`), and without it you cannot
redeploy to that address.

### A build others can verify

```sh
npx --no-install typesol build --docker
```

The same files, built inside a container instead of with your platform-tools. The container is made on your machine
from `docker/Dockerfile`, which ships in the package; every input is pinned: the Node and busybox base images by their
linux/amd64 digests, the Agave 3.1.10 and platform-tools v1.52 release files by sha256, the TypeSOL package (the
version your project uses) by its release record, `releases/<version>.json`: the npm tarball's sha512 integrity and
sha1 shasum and every file's sha256, checked before it is installed, and its npm dependencies (TypeScript, the
compiler's front end, among them) by that version's lock, `docker/deps/<version>.lock.json`, which `npm ci` installs
checking every package's integrity, with no install scripts. The lock of a version ships in the package of that
version (and in later ones); the locks of 0.43.0, 0.44.0 and 0.44.1, released before locks existed, were resolved
from the npm registry on 2026-11-12, so their integrity values are what the registry served then, not what an image
built at their release installed. The first `--docker` build of a TypeSOL version
builds the image (about 750 MB of downloads, a few minutes; Docker must be running, `typesol doctor` shows it); later
ones take seconds. The build runs with no network, the project mounted read-only, the output directory writable,
with no capabilities, as your uid and gid (root for a root caller). `my_app.build.json` then records the container:
the platform, the Dockerfile's sha256, the pinned base images and downloads, the TypeSOL tarball's hashes, the commit
its release record names, where the record came from (with the record's sha256), the dependency lock and its sha256,
and the local image id.

Deploy that `my_app.so` with the Solana CLI, `solana program deploy target/my_app/my_app.so --program-id
target/deploy/my_app-keypair.json --use-rpc` (with your `--url`). What replaces the container build: `typesol deploy`
(`--dry-run` included) and `typesol build` without `--docker`, which build again with your local platform-tools and
overwrite it; and `npm test` once the program's sources, SBPF version or address changed, which rebuilds it locally
and says so (`note: … held a --docker build that is out of date`). What does not: `npm test` while the sources are
the ones `my_app.build.json` records and the `.so` is the one it records, on any host: the tests then run the
container's binary. After a local build, `typesol build --docker` again before deploying. Commit the source, keep
`my_app.build.json`, and publish the commit and that file with the program id.

The TypeSOL inside the container is the version this `typesol` is, the one your project installs (`npx --no-install
typesol`); a global `typesol` of another version than the project's `node_modules/typesol` refuses rather than
guess. `--typesol-version <v>` picks another. Only versions with a release record can be installed (0.43.0 and later).
A package carries the records of the releases before it, because a release's record is written after it is
published; for a release the package does not record (the newest one, or a later one asked for), `--docker` fetches
`releases/<version>.json` from the repository's main branch
(`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/typesol-lang/typesol/main/releases/<version>.json`, unauthenticated HTTPS), prints
where it came from and its sha256, and records both in `my_app.build.json` (`container.typesol.record`). The check is
then two independent sources agreeing: the tarball npm serves must be the one the repository's record describes, so a
tampered package would have to be matched by a tampered repository. That holds for a fetched record and for a
`--release-record` file; for a version whose record ships in the running package, the record came from npm too (in
an earlier package), so the check is then against what npm served before. Offline, or when the repository has no
record for that version, it is an error that names `--release-record <file>`, which passes the record yourself (from
a checkout, `releases/<version>.json`). Between `npm publish` and the commit of the release's record the repository
answers HTTP 404: `--release-record` is the way then.

## 3. A wallet with SOL

```sh
solana-keygen new -o ~/.config/solana/deployer.json
solana config set --url mainnet-beta --keypair ~/.config/solana/deployer.json
solana address
```

Send SOL to that address. Most of what a deploy costs is rent for the program's bytes, which you get back if you
ever close the program:

```sh
solana rent $(wc -c < target/my_app/my_app.so)
```

For the counter that is about 0.080 SOL (rent is (128 + size) × 6,960 lamports at the current rate: 80,234,880
lamports for 11,400 bytes; the program data account holds 45 bytes more). During the deploy the program is first
written to a buffer account that holds the same amount again; it is returned when the deploy finishes. Fund about
twice the rent plus 0.01 SOL for fees: 0.17 SOL for the counter.

The public mainnet RPC is rate-limited; for deploys, set `--url` (or `solana config set --url`) to your RPC
provider's endpoint.

## 4. Deploy

```sh
npx --no-install typesol deploy --dry-run   # builds and prints the solana command it will run
npx --no-install typesol deploy
```

It runs `solana program deploy` at the address in `target/deploy/my_app-keypair.json`, with your wallet as payer and
upgrade authority, and prints the program id. Deploying again upgrades the program in place.

If a deploy stops part-way, the buffer stays behind with its SOL. The error prints the buffer's address; recover it
with `solana program close <buffer address>`, or list yours with `solana program show --buffers`.

## 5. Publish the IDL

```sh
npx --no-install typesol idl publish
```

It writes the IDL to the Program Metadata program, signed by the upgrade authority, where Anchor clients and
explorers look for it. It costs a few thousandths of a SOL of rent.

## 6. Verify

```sh
npx --no-install typesol verify my_app
```

`verify` rebuilds the program from `programs/my_app.ts`, reads the deployed one at the address in `typesol.json` from
the cluster in your Solana CLI config, and compares the bytes. `match` means anyone with your source and the same
TypeSOL version and toolchain gets exactly the program on chain (from 0.45.0 on, on any of the hosts measured: macOS arm64, Linux arm64 with the platform-tools `linux-aarch64` package as in [troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md#linux-arm64-the-agave-installer-fails-with-a-404), Linux x86_64; with 0.44.1 or earlier, a
program with 128-bit or signed division also needs the same kind of host). It also prints the upgrade authority and checks the IDL you published in step 5.

A match says only that the deployed bytes are what this source and this compiler build. It does not say that the
program, or the compiler, is correct, and it does not hold after the next upgrade: whoever holds the upgrade authority
it prints can replace the program at any time.

### Verifying someone else's program

With the source at the deployed commit, the program id and, ideally, the deployer's `<name>.build.json`:

```sh
git clone <repository> && cd <repository> && git checkout <commit>
npx --no-install typesol verify my_app --address <program id> --url mainnet-beta --docker --manifest my_app.build.json
```

`--docker` rebuilds in the same container recipe, built on your machine from the Dockerfile and checked inputs. The
TypeSOL version is the deployed build's (from the manifest whose binary hash is the deployed bytes'), or
`--typesol-version <v>`; months later, the current `@typesol/cli` installs the old version in the container, checked
against its release record. On a match it prints what was verified: the program, the source directory and its git
commit (and whether it has uncommitted changes), the TypeSOL version and tarball, the commit its record names and
where the record came from, the dependency lock and its sha256, the clang and platform-tools, the container's
Dockerfile sha256, base images and downloads, and the command that repeats it (with every option given that changes
the result: `--address`, `--url`, `--config`, `--sbpf`, `--manifest`, `--release-record`). A program built with
0.44.x on macOS or Linux arm64 that calls 128-bit or signed division does not match a `--docker` rebuild (those
versions' binaries depended on the host package; [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)). On a mismatch it shows the
toolchain of each side that is known, as without `--docker`. Exit codes: 0 match, 3 mismatch.

What this is not: the container is built locally from pinned inputs, not pulled from a published image, so the first
verification downloads the inputs and builds it. Its local image id can differ between machines; the Dockerfile's
sha256 and the pinned inputs are what to compare. The result is not registered with an external verified-build
registry: the evidence is the command and its output, which anyone can rerun.

## 7. Call it

`target/my_app/my_app.client.ts` builds the program's instructions on `@solana/kit`; see [client.md](client.md).

## Later

- **Upgrade it.** `typesol deploy` again replaces the code at the same address; the accounts keep their bytes. If an
  account struct changed, existing accounts do not match it. Only the size is checked (at least the struct's): a field
  added fails with 3003 on an account exactly the old size. On one created with spare space or grown since, it passes
  with no error: an appended field reads the spare bytes (zero unless written), and an inserted one makes the fields
  after it read other fields' bytes. A field removed from the middle, or moved, also reads other fields' bytes without
  an error. Migrate the accounts ([migrating an account](language-accounts.md#migrating-an-account)).
- **Freeze it.** `solana program set-upgrade-authority <program id> --final` makes the program immutable. It cannot
  be undone.
- **Close it.** `solana program close <program id> --bypass-warning` returns the rent to the authority. The program
  id can never be used again.

A worked example: the official escrow, deployed to mainnet in TypeSOL, Pinocchio, native Rust and Anchor, with every
transaction linked, is in the README's [On mainnet](../README.md#on-mainnet) section.

<!-- docs/security-model.md -->

# Security model

What a program compiled by TypeSOL can rely on, who is trusted, and what is left to the program's author. This is the
specification the tests check and an audit measures the compiler against; [audit.md](audit.md) is the package for
auditors, [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md) how to report a problem.

## Trust

| Party | Trusted for |
| --- | --- |
| The program's author | the program's logic: what it allows, to whom, for how much |
| TypeSOL (this repository) | that the binary does what the source and these guarantees say, and nothing an attacker can steer beyond it |
| The toolchain | the TypeScript compiler API (parsing, types), Agave platform-tools (clang, lld), Node.js. The guarantees are tested with one platform-tools release (v1.52, from Agave 3.1.10); a build with another warns, or fails with `--toolchain-strict`, and `<name>.build.json` records which one built a binary and on which host. The compiler builtins (128-bit multiplication, division and shifts, signed 64-bit division) are TypeSOL's own (`runtime/typesol_builtins.c`), compiled with the program; nothing is linked from platform-tools' Rust libraries, whose layout differed by host package, so from 0.45.0 on the programs measured build to the same bytes on macOS arm64, Linux arm64 and Linux x86_64 ([stability.md](stability.md#what-builds-the-same-bytes-where): 76 programs for SBPF v0, 14 for v1 and v2). `--docker` builds pin the whole environment in one linux/amd64 container whose inputs are checked by digest, checksum and integrity (base images, release files, the TypeSOL tarball and every npm dependency) |
| The Solana runtime | account ownership and signer flags as passed, the loader's account serialization, CPI privilege rules, sysvars |

Everything a transaction carries is attacker-controlled: the instruction data, which accounts are passed in which
slots (any account, repeated or not), the flags the runtime then enforces, the data of accounts the program does not
own, remaining accounts, and what another program returns or writes.

## Guarantees

Each holds for every instruction of every program the compiler accepts. A break of any of them is a security bug
(SECURITY.md).

### Before the body runs

1. **Account count.** Fewer accounts than parameters fail (3005); more than the program takes (32, or its `MAX_ACCOUNTS`) fail before parsing (5113).
2. **Account types.** Each parameter is checked for what its type says: `Signer` signed (3010); `Mut<…>` writable
   (2000); a program account (`Account<T>`, `Mut<T>`) initialized (3012), owned by this program (3007), at least
   `T`'s size (3003) and with `T`'s discriminator (3002), checked in that order; a `TokenAccount` / `Mint` an
   initialized account of that kind of SPL Token or Token-2022 (3012 for an empty system account (never created, or closed), 3007 for an account of another program, 3003 for a token program's account that is not an initialized token account (or mint) of its length); program parameters at their fixed address and executable
   (3008 / 3009); `SystemAccount` owned by the System Program (3011); `Zeroed<T>` owned, all-zero discriminator and
   rent-exempt.
3. **No aliasing.** Two writable parameters are never the same account (2040), whatever slots the transaction uses,
   unless the program marks one `Dup<…>`, and then only for accounts read and written in place (see below).
4. **Arguments.** Every argument is length-checked before it is read; strings are valid UTF-8; booleans, enums and
   options have valid tags (102).
5. **Constraints.** `Seeds` (2006, with the stored or the canonical bump), `Ata` (2015 / 2009 / 2014), `HasOne`
   (2001), `Owner` (2004), `Executable` (2007), `Address` (2012), `TokenOf` / `MintOf` (2014–2017, 2021, 2022) hold
   before the body, per account in Anchor's order ([errors.md](errors.md#which-error-a-transaction-gets)). A
   constraint naming an optional account is refused at compile time, so leaving the account out cannot skip it.

### While it runs

6. **Arithmetic.** Every `+ - * / % **`, compound assignment, `++` / `--`, unary minus, shift and cast is checked:
   overflow and lost bits fail (5100), division by zero fails (5101), a cast out of range fails (4102). There is no
   unchecked integer operation in the language.
7. **Bounds.** Every index into an array, Vec, FixedVec or remaining-account list is checked (5104); a
   growable Vec's stored length is checked against the account's size before it is used (3003).
8. **Account creation.** `create` / `createIfNeeded` is a top-level statement, and the account cannot be read or
   written before it (compile error). Creation refuses an account that already exists (the System Program's
   own error, custom 0; `initAccount<T>` over an account already holding a T is 3000), and an address someone
   pre-funded still gets created. `createIfNeeded` on an existing account re-derives the canonical PDA and checks
   owner, discriminator and size (token accounts: mint and owner; mints: decimals, authorities and the extensions it
   names). A `Migrate<From, To>` account is checked as an existing `From`; `migrate(…)` is a top-level statement every
   path reaches, builds the new value before rewriting the bytes, and nothing reads the old data after it (compile
   errors).
9. **Writes through references.** A place is never written after the code that computes its value may have moved it:
   replacing or resizing what a live reference points into is a compile error, as is writing a Vec element with a
   right side that may resize the Vec. A helper given a writable struct account may replace anything in it, however
   the account is named at the call (a parameter, an account group's field, a struct loaded with `loadAccountMut`): a
   reference into it read after the call is a compile error. Data that moves (a Vec of the account resized, so the
   Vecs after it shift, or a helper given the account) moves under every name of the account: a reference made
   through another parameter that may be the same account (a `Dup<…>` pair, a read-only and a writable account of one
   type, a struct loaded with `loadAccount` / `loadAccountMut`) is held to the same rule. A helper that can write gets its Pubkey, Option and
   string arguments as they were at the call (a copy unless nothing it is given reaches them), and a closed account
   is not used after `close()` (compile error).
10. **Remaining accounts.** Writing one (`.lamports`, `loadAccountMut`) checks it is writable (3006) and not another
    account of the instruction (2040); `loadAccountMut` loads a given account once per instruction (2040);
    `loadAccount<T>` checks owner, discriminator and size, and validates the data as instruction arguments are.
11. **Growth.** An account grows by at most 10 KiB per instruction (3016), counted from its length when the
    instruction started, the payer is a `Mut<Signer>`, new bytes are zero and the new rent is paid; shrinking keeps
    the lamports in the account.
12. **CPIs.** A program signs only for its own PDAs (the runtime enforces it; the seeds are those written in the
    source, with the values they had where the list was written, also for a named list or one given to a helper; a
    wrapper's arguments are evaluated left to right, as JS evaluates them, the seeds after the arguments before
    them). Token-2022 and SPL Token instruction data is laid out as the program reads it (a `COption` key that is
    None is one byte). `invoke` marks an account writable or signer only when the parameter is `Mut` / `Signer` or the program
    signs for it; remaining accounts keep the flags they were passed with, or are checked for the role requested.
    `invokeInstruction` is the exception by design: its program, account flags and data come from values (stored in
    account data or passed in), so the compiler cannot check them; the runtime does, refusing any account the
    transaction did not pass that way and any signer the program's seeds do not cover. Only programs that store
    instructions to run (a multisig, a DAO) need it; review who can write those values.
    Return data is read only from the program named, at the expected size (5106).
13. **Events.** `emitCpi` is accepted only from this program's event-authority PDA, signed (2002).

### When it ends

14. **Closing.** A `CloseTo<…>` or `close(…)` account has its lamports moved to the destination, its data zeroed and
    its owner reset to the System Program on every successful return, so it cannot be revived as the same account.
15. **No silent success.** Every failed check returns its error code and the transaction fails: no code path continues
    or returns success after a failed check or CPI.

## Left to the author

- **Logic.** Who may call what, limits, prices, fees. TypeSOL checks what the types and constraints say, nothing more.
- **`AccountInfo` / `UncheckedProgram`.** Unchecked by design, as in Anchor: check what you rely on.
- **`requirePda(account, seeds, bump)`.** Any valid bump passes (Anchor's `bump = expr`). Use a stored bump, never one
  from the arguments.
- **`Dup<…>`.** A parameter marked `Dup` may be the same account as another writable one. Reads see every write
  (both are the same bytes), so a value read before a write through the other slot is stale: read, then write. (A
  reference held across a resize through the other slot is a compile error, guarantee 9.)
- **`NATIVE_ACCOUNT_WRITES`.** A program that declares it gives up the up-front writability check and the
  one-view-per-account refusal for `loadRawMut`, `storeBorsh` and BigVec writes, as a native program has neither: the
  runtime still refuses a changed read-only account, but two loads of one account alias each other. Make the
  original's address and type checks before loading.
- **Instruction introspection.** The Instructions sysvar holds what the transaction's author put there. Require things
  of the transaction with it (that a repay instruction follows), never treat it as proof of who did what.
- **Oracles.** `pythPrice` checks the owner and account type, full verification, the feed id, the age and (when
  passed) the exponent; the raw `update.*` fields are unchecked. `switchboardValue` checks the owner, the account
  type, the expected feed, the sample count (`minSamples`, default 1) and staleness, measured in slots from the
  feed's `result.slot`. Neither checks, and both leave to the author:
  - the price's sign and zero: a negative or zero price is returned as it is;
  - the confidence: Pyth's `conf` and Switchboard's spread of samples are not compared with anything;
  - a publish time (Pyth) or result slot (Switchboard) in the future: it counts as fresh;
  - rounding: `switchboardValue` scales the 18-decimal result to `decimals` rounding toward zero, and a price scaled
    by its exponent in the program rounds as that code does.
- **`merkleVerify`.** Leaves and inner nodes hash alike: build leaves as `keccak256(keccak256(data))` in the program.
- **Existing accounts in `createIfNeeded`.** An existing token account's delegate and close authority, and a mint's
  extensions the call does not name, are not checked (as in Anchor).
- **Seeds of variable length.** Two adjacent string seeds can collide (`"ab" + "c"` and `"a" + "bc"`), as in Anchor.

## Where TypeSOL is stricter than Anchor

- Any two writable parameters naming one account are refused unless one is `Dup<…>` (Anchor compares only program
  and token accounts, and `dup` lifts that).
- Arithmetic overflow returns an error code (5100) in every build; Anchor aborts the program, and only when
  overflow checks are enabled.

## Review of 0.44.0 (2026-11-11)

A second internal review, of 0.44.0, found guarantees 9 and 12 and the token wrappers' instruction data broken in the
cases listed in [audit.md](audit.md#0440-2026-11-11); they are fixed in 0.44.1. Of the 76 programs of the 0.44.0
sources, 74 build to the same binary with 0.44.1 and 2 to another (mint-close-authority and allow-block-list-token);
none is refused. A program was exposed only if it uses the construct a defect names:

- `mint.create` / `createIfNeeded` with `transferFee` whose config or withdraw authority is `null` or a run-time None
  (the mint got another fee and no withdraw authority: check the mint), or extensions adding up to 355 bytes (the
  call always failed);
- a `Dup<…>` pair, a read-only and a writable account of one struct type, or a struct loaded with `loadAccount` /
  `loadAccountMut`, with a reference made through one held across a push, pop or clear (or a helper given the
  account) through the other, when the transaction passes one account for both;
- a token or Stake wrapper call with signer seeds and an argument that runs code (a helper call, an assignment) whose
  effects the seeds, the amount or a metadata string read;
- `updateExtraAccountMetas` after the account was already grown in the same instruction.

A program that uses none of them was not exposed to these defects; rebuilding it with 0.44.1 gives the same binary.

## Review of 0.43.0 (2026-11-11)

An internal review of 0.43.0 found that some of the guarantees above did not hold in every case; the defects are
listed in [audit.md](audit.md#0430-2026-11-11) and fixed in 0.44.0. Programs built with 0.43.0 or
earlier should be rebuilt with it and redeployed: the fixes change the binary of programs that have a helper
taking a Pubkey, Option, string or u256, exposed or not (35 of the 76 programs of the 0.43.0 sources build to the same
binary, 41 to another).

The defect that can break an authorization check is the first: a Pubkey, Option, string or u256 argument of a
helper was not a copy. A program was exposed where all of these hold:

- a helper takes a parameter of one of those types and also an account it writes (or remaining accounts, or an
  `Inout` place);
- a call passes that parameter a field of the same account (`rotate(v, v.admin, caller)`), or a value stored in it;
- the helper reads the parameter after writing the field (`v.admin = v.pending`, then a check on `admin`): it read
  the new value;
- the helper was not inlined. A `/** @noinline */` helper never is; for the others it was clang's choice, which the
  source does not show, so count every such call as exposed.

Each of the other defects needs the construct it names: a seed list bound to a name, given to a helper or written
beside an argument with side effects; a reference held across a helper that is given an account-group field or a
loaded account; Borsh input with an Option of a struct that holds an Option (a bounded read past the input, no
write); a closure or callback that changes a local read before it; a string viewing an `Inout` place; `close()` into
the account itself, `Dup<…>` on a closed account, or an account used after `close()`. A program without them was not
exposed to them.

## Status

The compiler and runtime have had internal security reviews, the latest of 0.44.0 (above); its findings are fixed in
0.44.1. It was an internal review, not an independent audit; it covered the token, Token-2022, Metaplex and Stake
wrappers, the oracles and SBPF v1/v2 builds of the examples that the review of 0.43.0 left out, but not the Metaplex
wrappers for unusual argument shapes beyond reading them, the large ports on SBPF v1/v2, or Windows. There has been no
external audit: see [audit.md](audit.md).

<!-- docs/ai.md -->

# Writing TypeSOL with an AI agent

TypeSOL is TypeScript, which AI coding agents write well, but a subset of it: a model's ordinary habits (`1` for an
integer, `console.log`, `throw`, `xs[i]`) are refused. Four things close that gap.

## The rules in the project

`typesol init` writes the rules an agent needs into the project:

| File | Read by |
| --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md` | Codex, Cursor, Zed, Aider and other agents that read AGENTS.md |
| `CLAUDE.md` (`@AGENTS.md`) | Claude Code |
| `.cursor/rules/typesol.mdc` | Cursor (always applied to `programs/` and `tests/`) |

They say what ordinary TypeScript habits break (bigint integers, imports from `"typesol"`, no `throw` / `async` /
`class`, `Mut<T>` for an account that changes, `.get(i)` / `.set(i, v)` on lists) and how to check and test. Keep your
own project notes below them in AGENTS.md. `typesol init --no-agent-files` leaves these files and the MCP
configuration below out.

## llms.txt

[typesol.com/llms.txt](https://typesol.com/llms.txt) is the index of the docs for models
([llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org)); [llms-full.txt](https://typesol.com/llms-full.txt) is the rules, the quick start
and the reference (language, errors, tests, CLI, client, porting from Anchor, troubleshooting, mainnet, security model)
in one file, to paste into a chat or give to a model as context. Both also ship in the npm package
(`node_modules/typesol/llms-full.txt` in a project `typesol init` created, which installs `@typesol/cli` under the
name `typesol`; `node_modules/@typesol/cli/llms-full.txt` where it is installed under its own name).

## Errors an agent can fix by itself

`typesol check --json` prints `{ "ok": false, "diagnostics": [...] }`; each diagnostic has `file`, `line`, `column`,
`length`, `message` and, for the usual mistakes, `hint`: what to write instead ("integers (u64, u32, i64 …) are bigint
in TypeSOL: write 1n, not 1, and take u64, not number"). An agent can loop on check → edit → check without building.

## The MCP server

`typesol mcp` serves the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) on stdio. `typesol init` writes
`.mcp.json` (Claude Code) and `.cursor/mcp.json` (Cursor) that start it with `npx --no-install typesol mcp`: the
project's own copy, after `npm install`. `--no-install` matters: `typesol` is not the npm package's name, and without
it npx would fetch whatever package is published as `typesol` when the project's copy is missing. Other clients take
the same command, run in the project directory:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "typesol": { "command": "npx", "args": ["--no-install", "typesol", "mcp"] } } }
```

Outside a project, start it from the published package by its full name: `npx -y @typesol/cli mcp`.

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `check` | type-checks a program (`file`, or `source` text) and returns the diagnostics with their hints |
| `idl` | the Anchor-compatible IDL the program compiles to |
| `docs` | searches the docs and returns the best-matching sections |
| `rules` | the rules above |

Building and testing stay in the shell (`npm test`, `npx --no-install typesol build`): they need the platform-tools and write
files, which an agent should do in the open.

<!-- docs/stability.md -->

# Stability and the road to 1.0

TypeSOL is pre-1.0. Until 1.0, a minor release (0.x → 0.y) may change the language, the account and IDL layout of
generated programs and error codes, and says so in the CHANGELOG ([versioning
policy](https://github.com/typesol-lang/.github/blob/main/VERSIONING.md)). This page says what 1.0 will promise, which
parts are already meant to stay as they are, and what has to be settled first.

## What 1.0 will promise

From 1.0 on, within a major version:

- **Sources keep compiling.** A program that compiles with 1.x compiles with every later 1.y, to a program with the same
  account layouts, IDL, instruction and account discriminators and error codes. New releases add; they do not take away.
- **Binaries are reproducible and only change for a reason.** With the same TypeSOL release and the tested
  toolchain, a source builds to the same bytes in the build container (`--docker`) as on the hosts measured: from
  0.45.0 on, macOS arm64, Linux arm64 and Linux x86_64, for the programs and SBPF versions listed
  [below](#what-builds-the-same-bytes-where).
  A release that changes the binary of a program that uses none of its new features says so, with the release
  manifest's diff (`typesol-<version>-binary-diff.txt`) as the evidence.
- **The checks stay.** No check a program gets from its parameter types (owner, discriminator, signer, writability,
  aliasing, checked arithmetic, constraints) is removed or weakened.
- **The tools keep their interfaces**: `typesol build`, `test` (via `typesol/testing`), `check --json`, `deploy`,
  `verify`, `idl`, the typed client, and `typesol.json`.

## Stable already

Meant to stay as they are; a change before 1.0 would be a breaking change listed as one:

- Types: the integers (`u8` … `u128`, `i8` … `i128`), `boolean`, `Pubkey`, `Hash`, structs, `FixedArray`, `FixedVec`,
  `Vec`, `FixedString`, `Option`, unit and data enums, `u256` in computation.
- Account parameters and their checks: `Signer`, `Account<T>`, `Mut<T>`, `Init<T>`, `InitIfNeeded<T>`, `Zeroed<T>`,
  optional accounts, token accounts and mints, programs, sysvars, account groups; the constraints (`HasOne`, `Seeds`,
  `CloseTo`, `Ata`, `Address`, `Owner`, `Executable`).
- Errors and events: error enums and their codes, `require`, `AnchorError`, `emit`, `emitCpi`.
- CPIs: System, SPL Token, Token-2022, Associated Token, Memo, generic `invoke` with PDA signing.
- Layouts: account data (Anchor's discriminator and fixed or `@layout borsh` layout), the IDL, the client.

## What a release gives you now

- **The npm package is the one that was checked.** From 0.43.0 on, `releases/<version>.json` in the repository holds
  the published tarball's shasum and integrity and every file's sha256, packed from a clean export of the release tag
  after install, build and lint. `npm pack` is reproducible here, so anyone can pack the tag again and compare, or
  compare the registry with `node scripts/release-check.ts <version> --verify --registry`
  ([docs/testing.md](testing.md#the-npm-tarball)).
- **The tests cover one toolchain.** Each release declares the Agave and platform-tools it is tested with
  (`TESTED_TOOLCHAIN`, exported from `typesol/compiler`; Agave 3.1.10 and platform-tools v1.52 now). A binary built with
  another clang is outside what the tests cover: `typesol build` and `deploy` warn once, `--toolchain-strict` (or
  `TYPESOL_TOOLCHAIN=strict`) refuses it, and `typesol doctor` shows which one is active.
- **A build says what made it.** `<name>.build.json` records the TypeSOL, TypeScript, clang and platform-tools versions,
  the host, the SBPF version and the sha256 of every source and of the binary. `typesol verify` uses it to say, on a
  mismatch, whether the toolchains differ. A program on chain records none of this: keep the file with the deployment.
- **A deployed program anyone can rebuild.** `typesol build --docker` builds in a container made from
  `docker/Dockerfile` (in the package), whose inputs are all pinned: base images by digest, the Agave and
  platform-tools release files by sha256, the TypeSOL tarball by its `releases/<version>.json`. `typesol verify
  --docker` rebuilds there and says what it verified. The image is built locally from those inputs; no image is
  published, and the result is not registered with any external verified-build registry
  ([docs/mainnet.md](mainnet.md#6-verify)).
- **Fixes come as patches of the latest minor.** From 0.44.0 on, a release that only fixes soundness or security
  defects is a patch (0.44.1, …) with no new language surface, and its notes carry the binary diff against the
  previous release ([SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md#fix-releases)). Older minors are not maintained.

## What builds the same bytes where

From 0.45.0 on, the programs measured build to the same bytes on each host measured. Measured with this release's
compiler and platform-tools v1.52 on macOS arm64 (the platform-tools `osx-aarch64` package, native), Linux arm64 and
Linux x86_64 (the `linux-aarch64` and `linux-x86_64` packages, in containers; x86_64 is the `--docker` image; Linux
arm64 has no Agave CLI, so there the package is set up by hand with `TYPESOL_SBF_SDK`, as in
[troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md#linux-arm64-the-agave-installer-fails-with-a-404)): for
SBPF v0 (the default), the 76 programs of the sources (`scripts/release-manifest.ts`, every program under `examples/`
and `showcase/`); for SBPF v1 and v2, the 14 programs of `test/golden/binaries.json` (counter, vault, escrow, multisig
and the 10 below).

| What | Same on the three hosts? |
| --- | --- |
| The generated C and the IDL (all 76) | yes |
| The binary, SBPF v0 (all 76) | yes |
| The binary, SBPF v1 and v2 (the 14) | yes |
| The binary, SBPF v0, against 0.44.1 | 66 programs build to 0.44.1's bytes on each of the three; the 10 below build to new bytes, the same on the three |
| The binary, SBPF v1 and v2, against 0.44.1 (on macOS arm64) | v1: all 14 build to new bytes; v2: 9 (the 10 below but token-fundraiser) build to new bytes, the other 5 (counter, vault, escrow, multisig, token-fundraiser) to 0.44.1's |

The 10 are the programs that call 128-bit or signed 64-bit division (the Phoenix, Marginfi, Raydium AMM, CLMM and
CP-Swap, Jito priority-fee and Stake Pool ports, transfer-fee, token-fundraiser, token-swap). With 0.44.1 each of them
built to three different binaries on the three hosts (token-fundraiser: the two Linux ones agreed). The cause was one
library: platform-tools' SBF `compiler-builtins` Rust library (`libcompiler_builtins-<hash>.rlib`, a different file in
each host package). Its functions have the same instructions in the three packages (compared function by function for
SBPF v0, v1 and v2), but each package splits them into differently numbered archive members, so the linker placed the
ones a division pulls in (`__udivti3`, its shared `u128_div_rem`, `__ashlti3`, `__lshrti3`, …) in another order, and
the program's calls into them had other offsets. Programs that called at most `__multi3` linked one member and agreed.

TypeSOL now links none of that library: `runtime/typesol_builtins.c` defines every builtin the tested clang calls for
C integer code on SBF (`__multi3`, `__udivti3`, `__umodti3`, `__divti3`, `__modti3`, `__ashlti3`, `__lshrti3`, `__ashrti3`, `__divdi3`,
`__moddi3`) and is compiled with each program, by the same clang, and linked after it. Multiplication and shifts are
the instructions compiler-builtins has for them, so on SBPF v0 programs that use only those keep their bytes;
division is new C that costs no more compute units than compiler-builtins' on any input measured, and fewer on most
(`test/language/builtins.test.ts`). On SBPF v1, `__multi3` (128-bit multiplication, which checked 64-bit
multiplication uses too) is C as well, cheaper than compiler-builtins' there (175 against 177.5 compute units a call on average in that test),
so a v1 program that
multiplies that way builds to other bytes than with 0.44.1 (every one of the 14 measured does); SBPF v2 multiplies
with its own instructions and calls no `__multi3`, and its signed 64-bit division is an instruction too, which is
why token-fundraiser keeps its v2 bytes.
libc's `memcpy` and `memset` still come from platform-tools; the programs that link them build the same on the three
hosts. Nothing in the emitted C, the paths or the build directory reaches the binary.

The reference environment stays one platform, so that the whole environment is one recipe: the build container is
`linux/amd64` on every machine (emulated on arm64 hosts). CI checks on every change that a Linux x86_64 runner with
independently installed platform-tools builds the programs of `test/golden/binaries.json` (the 14 for SBPF v0, and
counter, escrow, Phoenix and Marginfi for v1 and v2) to the container's bytes; that is the same host package as the
container's, installed separately. The macOS workflow (on demand) runs the same check on macOS arm64, and anyone can
run it on another host, binary included. `<name>.build.json` records the host; `typesol verify` counts a host
difference between builds made before 0.45.0 (which linked compiler-builtins: a possible cause if the program uses
128-bit or signed division), and between later builds only when one of the hosts is not among the three measured
(`host (not measured)`).

## Experimental

Useful today, but may still change before 1.0 (each change listed in the CHANGELOG):

- The native-program surface (0.40.0): `loadRaw` / `loadRawMut`, the instruction data readers, error code 0,
  `ProgramError`, `panic`, `PANIC_ON_OVERFLOW`, `ERROR_LOG_PREFIX` / `PROGRAM_ERROR_LOG_PREFIX`, `logBase64`,
  `createProgramAddress`.
- `loadBorsh` / `storeBorsh` (0.42.0): a native program's Borsh accounts read into a local struct and written back.
- `BigVec<T>` (0.42.0): SPL's `big_vec`, a list over the rest of a native account.
- Views at run-time offsets (0.43.0): `loadRawAt` / `loadRawMutAt`, `rawArrayAt` / `rawArrayMutAt`; a read-only
  view read where it is made (`loadRaw<T>(a).field`, `rbTreeAt(…).length`), and the owner check's cache the views share.
- The built-in RedBlackTree (0.43.0): `rbTreeAt` / `rbTreeMutAt`, lib-sokoban 0.3's byte layout and algorithms,
  its panics in solana-program 1.14–1.17's format, `removeAt(index)` (what it gives for a node in no tree may change).
- `panic(null, location)` (no log line) and `abort()` (Rust's abort, "SBF program panicked") (0.42.0).
- Failures without a log line (0.43.0): `ERROR_LOG_PREFIX = null` / `PROGRAM_ERROR_LOG_PREFIX = null`.
- `findProgramAddressWithBump` (0.43.0), with `const [address, bump] = …` its only array destructuring.
- Plain type aliases (0.43.0): `type Price = u64`, replaced by the type they name.
- File-local structs (0.43.0): `interface Pair { … }` without `export`, for helpers and locals, out of the IDL.
- Constant expressions (0.43.0): top-level integer constants folded from literals and earlier constants, a typed
  one computed in its type.
- Comma-separated `for` updates and initializers (0.43.0).
- Stack room (0.43.0): `/** @noinline */` helpers and `/** @heap */` locals.
- Local `FixedVec` / `FixedArray` lists of structs, `FixedVec.pushAll`, the instruction data as a list (`slice`,
  `InstructionBytes` helper parameters), `invokeInstruction` in helpers (0.42.0); local FixedVecs given for read-only
  `FixedVec<T, N>` / `Vec<T>` helper parameters (0.43.0).
- `epochRewards()` and `EpochRewards` (0.42.0): the EpochRewards sysvar through its syscall.
- `NATIVE_ACCOUNT_WRITES` (0.42.0): opt-in native write semantics for `loadRawMut`, `storeBorsh` and BigVec writes
  (writability and aliasing left to the runtime). It drops checks a program would otherwise get, so it stays outside
  "the checks stay" promise above: it only applies to programs that declare it.
- `Inout<T>` helper parameters (0.43.0): a helper that changes a struct, FixedArray or FixedVec of the caller's
  that is not an account (a local, a `loadBorsh` local, a field of a `loadRawMut` view, a list element), with the
  aliasing rules at each call. It settles the open edge of helpers taking a writable struct that is not an account,
  which were refused; the rules (what counts as overlapping, which places may move) may still be refined.
- For native ports (0.43.0): `setReturnData` and `logComputeUnits` in a native entry; `closeRaw`, `assignOwner`
  and `resizeAccount` on remaining accounts; the byte builders of `FixedVec<u8, N>` (`pushLE`, `pushKey`, `pushBorsh`,
  `setLE`, `truncate`); `PANIC_STYLE = "solana-1.14"` and `panicsAt(location, expression)`.
- Metaplex CPIs (Token Metadata, Core, Bubblegum), oracles (Pyth, Switchboard), the Stake program.
- `programAt<P>` / `sysvarAt<S>` and remaining accounts in the typed CPIs (System, Token, ATA, Memo, Stake); a ternary
  between remaining accounts and `AccountInfo` parameters (0.42.0).
- Functions chosen at run time and lists of functions, closures returned from functions.
- `typesol/testing`'s epochs and staking: `warpToEpoch`, `nextEpoch`, `StakeCluster`, `stakeActivation`, the vote and
  stake account builders and `readStakeAccount`.
- Tools: `typesol port`, `clone`, `profile`, `cpi`, the editor plugin, the MCP server and the agent files `init`
  writes, the SBPF v1 and v2 targets.

## Before 1.0

- **An external audit** of the compiler and runtime ([audit package](audit.md)), its findings fixed and published.
- **Settle the open edges**, each either supported or refused with a clear error:
  - a struct holding a FixedVec as both an argument and account data (two layouts, one IDL type);
  - `require` with an error code computed at run time that is 0: fails as an overflow (5100) today, where a native
    program returns CUSTOM_ZERO;
  - which experimental parts above become stable, and which stay outside the 1.0 promise.
- **A release candidate** (1.0.0-rc) used for the showcase ports and the templates, with no breaking change between it
  and 1.0.0.
